prevention: Write authorization tests for cross-tenant access, use tenant-aware repository patterns and audit sensitive access. Treat tenant context as security-critical data.

title: A distributed lock is held after the worker crashes
short: A distributed lock should reduce overlap, not be the only protection against duplicate execution.
answer: I would use a lease with an owner token and safe renewal. If the worker dies, the lease expires and another worker can continue. The job must still be idempotent because distributed locks cannot provide perfect failure exclusion.
code: Use a lock with a unique owner token and bounded lease. Renew it only while the worker is healthy, and release only when the token matches. Make the job itself idempotent because lease expiry can still allow another worker to take over.
followups: What happens during a network partition?
mistakes: Using a lock with no expiry.
Releasing a lock without verifying ownership.
interview: I use leases for recovery and idempotency for correctness. The lock is an optimization for coordination, not the sole business guarantee.
scenario: A scheduled job acquires a distributed lock and the process crashes before releasing it. Other workers stop processing the job.
investigation: Check lock ownership, TTL and renewal behavior. Determine whether the lock can expire safely and whether a worker can accidentally release another worker’s lock.
resolution: Use a lock with a unique owner token and bounded lease. Renew it only while the worker is healthy, and release only when the token matches. Make the job itself idempotent because lease expiry can still allow another worker to take over.
prevention: Test crashes, long-running jobs and clock/network issues. Monitor stale locks and job execution overlap.

title: A service becomes overloaded even though request rate is normal
short: Backpressure means the system limits work to what downstream capacity can sustain.
answer: I would cap concurrency and queue depth so slow downstream calls cannot consume all resources. Then I would add timeouts and bulkheads and decide which work can be rejected, delayed or moved asynchronously.
code: Apply bounded concurrency and queue sizes, reject or shed excess work, set timeouts and isolate slow dependencies with bulkheads. Prefer asynchronous processing when the business flow allows it.
followups: How does a bounded queue protect a service?
When should requests be rejected with 429 or 503?
How do virtual threads change this analysis?
mistakes: Using unbounded executor queues.
Assuming more threads always improve throughput.
interview: The service is overloaded by waiting work, not necessarily by incoming request count. I would control concurrency and queue growth first.
scenario: Traffic volume is steady, but a downstream dependency becomes slower. Worker threads accumulate waiting on I/O and memory usage rises until the service becomes unhealthy.
investigation: Inspect active threads, executor queue depth, request concurrency, downstream latency and memory. Look for unbounded queues and synchronous blocking calls.
resolution: Apply bounded concurrency and queue sizes, reject or shed excess work, set timeouts and isolate slow dependencies with bulkheads. Prefer asynchronous processing when the business flow allows it.
prevention: Monitor saturation signals, load-test dependency slowness and define overload behavior explicitly instead of allowing unbounded waiting.

title: A downstream timeout is shorter than the upstream timeout
short: Timeouts should form a coherent deadline budget, not independent arbitrary numbers.
answer: I would define a total request deadline and allocate smaller budgets to downstream calls. When the deadline is exceeded, the work should be cancelled or abandoned safely so the system does not keep consuming capacity for a request that no longer matters.
code: Use an end-to-end deadline budget. Each downstream call must have a timeout less than the remaining deadline, and cancellation should propagate where the protocol supports it.
followups: How do you propagate deadlines over HTTP?
What if the downstream operation is not cancellable?
How does this relate to retries?
mistakes: Giving every dependency a fixed large timeout.
Ignoring work that continues after client timeout.
interview: I treat timeouts as a budget. Every downstream dependency must respect the remaining deadline.
scenario: The gateway allows 5 seconds, Service A allows 4 seconds, but Service B allows 10 seconds. Requests keep running downstream after the caller has already timed out.
investigation: Map timeouts across the request chain and inspect work that continues after upstream cancellation. Measure wasted downstream work.
resolution: Use an end-to-end deadline budget. Each downstream call must have a timeout less than the remaining deadline, and cancellation should propagate where the protocol supports it.
prevention: Standardize timeout policies, propagate deadlines and test cancellation under load.

title: A feature flag causes inconsistent behavior across instances
short: Feature flags are distributed configuration and need consistency semantics just like any other configuration.
answer: I would first define the consistency requirement. For pricing, I may need user or transaction stickiness and a versioned flag. I would also expose the active configuration version so incidents can be correlated to rollout state.
code: Define whether the flag is evaluated per request, user or tenant. For correctness-sensitive changes, use versioned configuration and atomic rollout rules. Ensure all instances can report their active configuration.
followups: How would you roll back a bad flag?
What if a flag service is unavailable?
How do you make a transaction use one consistent flag value?
mistakes: Changing business-critical flags without auditability.
Assuming all instances update instantly.
interview: I would not treat feature flags as harmless UI switches. In backend systems they can change business behavior and need rollout, audit and consistency controls.
scenario: Half the instances use the new pricing algorithm and half use the old one because flag updates arrive at different times.
investigation: Check flag propagation latency, caching, evaluation rules and whether requests can move between instances during a session.
resolution: Define whether the flag is evaluated per request, user or tenant. For correctness-sensitive changes, use versioned configuration and atomic rollout rules. Ensure all instances can report their active configuration.
prevention: Audit flag changes, expose configuration version in diagnostics and define rollback behavior before enabling production flags.

title: An event consumer commits the database but crashes before acknowledging Kafka
short: Kafka offset management and database commits are separate systems; without a transaction bridge, duplicate delivery is normal.
answer: I would commit the business transaction first and acknowledge the message only after success. Because a crash can happen between those actions, the handler must be idempotent using a stable event ID or business uniqueness constraint.
code: Design the handler for at-least-once delivery. Use a unique event ID or business key to make the database operation idempotent, and acknowledge only after successful processing.
followups: How would you implement an inbox table?
What if the event has no stable ID?
mistakes: Assuming manual offset commit creates exactly once.
Acknowledging before the business transaction commits.
interview: I assume at-least-once delivery. The correctness mechanism is idempotent business processing, not hoping the consumer never crashes between commit and acknowledgement.
scenario: The consumer processes an event and commits a database transaction, then crashes before committing the Kafka offset. After restart the same event is delivered again.
investigation: Compare consumer offset progression with database transaction logs. Confirm whether the business effect is repeatable and whether an event ID is stored.
resolution: Design the handler for at-least-once delivery. Use a unique event ID or business key to make the database operation idempotent, and acknowledge only after successful processing.
prevention: Test crash windows between business commit and offset commit. Monitor duplicate delivery and keep stable event identifiers.

title: A cache stampede occurs after a popular key expires
short: A cache stampede is a synchronized miss that overwhelms the source of truth.
answer: I would prevent multiple callers from refreshing the same hot key concurrently, add TTL jitter and allow stale data when the business permits it. The database should also have a bounded fallback path.
code: Use request coalescing or a single-flight mechanism so only one request refreshes a key. Add TTL jitter and stale-while-revalidate where acceptable. Protect the source with bounded concurrency.
followups: How would you handle a cache miss when Redis is down?
mistakes: Using the same TTL for every hot key.
Letting every miss query the database.
interview: I would design for cache expiry as a failure mode. Request coalescing, TTL jitter and stale-while-revalidate are useful controls.
scenario: A popular product cache entry expires. Thousands of requests miss simultaneously and all query the database.
investigation: Look at cache-miss rate, database QPS and key popularity around the expiration time. Check whether TTLs are synchronized across instances.
resolution: Use request coalescing or a single-flight mechanism so only one request refreshes a key. Add TTL jitter and stale-while-revalidate where acceptable. Protect the source with bounded concurrency.
prevention: Monitor hot keys, avoid synchronized expirations and load-test cache expiry events rather than only steady-state cache hits.

title: A service discovery outage prevents new pods from finding dependencies
short: A control-plane failure should not immediately become a data-plane outage if safe cached state can keep traffic flowing.
answer: I would separate control-plane availability from data-plane traffic. Clients should cache usable discovery information for a bounded period, while the discovery system itself is highly available.
code: Use highly available discovery, client-side caching with bounded staleness and resilient DNS behavior. Ensure startup does not require an indefinitely available discovery control plane if existing endpoints can be reused safely.
followups: How does DNS caching affect recovery?
What happens when an instance IP changes?
mistakes: Making every request synchronously query discovery.
Ignoring stale discovery data.
interview: I would design discovery failure so existing traffic can continue for some bounded period instead of making every request depend on the control plane.
scenario: The service discovery component becomes unavailable. Existing connections continue to work, but newly started pods cannot resolve downstream services.
investigation: Check discovery health, DNS/cache behavior and whether clients cache resolved endpoints. Compare existing versus newly created instances.
resolution: Use highly available discovery, client-side caching with bounded staleness and resilient DNS behavior. Ensure startup does not require an indefinitely available discovery control plane if existing endpoints can be reused safely.
prevention: Test control-plane outages, monitor discovery availability and define how long clients can safely use cached endpoints.

title: A payment is charged but the order service records failure
short: External payment calls create an uncertain outcome; the safe design is idempotency plus reconciliation, not blind retry.
answer: I would never blindly retry a timed-out payment. I would use a stable idempotency key, query the provider for the existing result, persist the final state and reconcile unknown transactions asynchronously.
code: Use an idempotency key with the payment provider and persist the payment attempt state. On timeout, query the provider by idempotency key or transaction ID before retrying. Add reconciliation for uncertain states.
followups: How would you model payment states?
What if the provider does not support idempotency?
How do you reconcile thousands of pending payments?
mistakes: Treating timeout as proof that no charge happened.
Generating a new payment ID for every retry.
interview: Payment is a classic example where timeout does not mean failure. I need an idempotency key and a way to reconcile uncertain outcomes.
scenario: The payment provider confirms a charge, but the order service times out before recording the success. A retry risks charging the customer twice.
investigation: Trace the payment provider request and inspect provider transaction IDs. Determine whether the timeout happened before or after the provider committed the charge.
resolution: Use an idempotency key with the payment provider and persist the payment attempt state. On timeout, query the provider by idempotency key or transaction ID before retrying. Add reconciliation for uncertain states.
prevention: Persist provider IDs, model pending/unknown states, reconcile regularly and test timeouts after external commit.

title: A message schema change breaks consumers after deployment
short: Event schemas are contracts; changing them without compatibility rules is equivalent to breaking an API.
answer: I would treat the event schema as a versioned contract. I would prefer additive changes and enforce compatibility checks before deployment. If a breaking change is unavoidable, I would introduce a new version and migrate consumers deliberately.
code: Use explicit schema evolution rules. Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes, version schemas where necessary and use a schema registry or contract checks to reject incompatible producer changes.
mistakes: Changing field types casually.
Testing only the producer.
interview: I would put schema compatibility in the deployment pipeline so an incompatible event cannot reach production accidentally.
scenario: A producer changes a field type from integer to string. Some consumers deserialize the event successfully while older consumers fail.
investigation: Compare schema versions and consumer compatibility rules. Identify which consumers are still on older versions.
resolution: Use explicit schema evolution rules. Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes, version schemas where necessary and use a schema registry or contract checks to reject incompatible producer changes.
prevention: Run compatibility tests in CI and maintain a deprecation window for consumers before removing old fields or changing semantics.

title: @Async tasks overwhelm the application thread pool
short: Asynchrony changes where work waits; it does not remove capacity limits.
answer: I would use a dedicated bounded executor, measure task duration and choose a rejection or backpressure policy. For durable background work I would prefer a queue so work survives process restarts.
code: Use a dedicated bounded executor with an explicit queue and rejection policy. Size it for the workload, isolate unrelated task types and move durable long-running work to a message broker when necessary.
followups: How do you size a thread pool?
What happens when the executor queue is full?
When would Kafka be better than @Async?
mistakes: Using an unbounded queue.
Sharing one executor across unrelated workloads.
interview: I would not solve this by simply increasing the thread count. I would bound the executor and choose whether excess work should be rejected, delayed or persisted to messaging.
scenario: A new asynchronous feature submits thousands of tasks. The default executor queue grows, memory increases and request latency degrades.
investigation: Inspect executor active threads, queue depth, task duration and rejection count. Check whether tasks are CPU-bound or I/O-bound and whether callers need the work synchronously.
resolution: Use a dedicated bounded executor with an explicit queue and rejection policy. Size it for the workload, isolate unrelated task types and move durable long-running work to a message broker when necessary.
prevention: Monitor executor saturation and load-test bursts. Do not use one unbounded executor for unrelated workloads.

title: A transactional method calls an @Async method and data is missing
short: Spring transactions are thread-bound; asynchronous execution creates a different execution context.
answer: I would not rely on the async method seeing uncommitted transaction state. If the task needs committed data, I would trigger it after commit or use a durable event/message so the ordering is explicit.
code: Do not assume @Async inherits the transaction. Publish an event after commit or move the asynchronous work behind a durable queue. If direct async execution is acceptable, ensure the transaction has committed before the async work starts.
followups: How does @Transactional interact with thread pools?
How would you publish an event after commit?
mistakes: Assuming @Async inherits the transaction.
Starting background work before commit.
interview: A transaction does not automatically flow into @Async. Crossing the thread boundary means I need an explicit post-commit or messaging design.
scenario: A service saves an entity inside a transaction and then calls an asynchronous method that immediately queries the database. The async task sometimes cannot see the expected data.
investigation: Check transaction commit timing and thread boundaries. @Async executes on another thread, so it does not share the caller thread-bound transaction.
resolution: Do not assume @Async inherits the transaction. Publish an event after commit or move the asynchronous work behind a durable queue. If direct async execution is acceptable, ensure the transaction has committed before the async work starts.
prevention: Test commit/async race conditions and define whether the background task requires committed state or can operate on an in-memory command.

title: A Spring Boot application starts slowly after a new release
short: Startup performance should be measured by phase; otherwise teams tend to guess which bean is responsible.
answer: I would profile startup and compare bean initialization and external calls with the previous version. Then I would move non-critical work out of startup and reduce scanning or initialization only where measurements justify it.
code: Remove unnecessary scanning, defer non-critical initialization and move expensive startup work out of the critical path. Use lazy initialization selectively, not as a blanket fix.
followups: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration affect startup?
How would you debug a startup hang?
mistakes: Enabling lazy initialization everywhere without measuring.
Ignoring external calls during startup.
interview: I would profile first, because startup can be slow due to bean creation, database migration, classpath scanning or remote configuration.
scenario: Startup time increases from 15 seconds to 90 seconds after adding several dependencies and configuration classes.
investigation: Compare startup profiles between releases. Inspect bean creation, classpath scanning, database initialization, remote configuration and slow post-construct/startup tasks.
resolution: Remove unnecessary scanning, defer non-critical initialization and move expensive startup work out of the critical path. Use lazy initialization selectively, not as a blanket fix.
prevention: Track startup time as a deployment metric and keep startup dependencies deterministic. Profile before optimizing.

title: A controller returns 200 but the business operation failed
short: An HTTP success response is part of the business contract; swallowing failures can be worse than returning a 500.
answer: I would avoid catching exceptions merely to log them. Unexpected failures should reach centralized exception handling, which returns a consistent status and error body. Known business errors should map explicitly to meaningful 4xx responses.
code: Let unexpected exceptions propagate to a centralized exception handler and map them to appropriate status codes. Return a stable error contract with correlation information, not internal stack traces.
followups: When should a business error be 409 versus 400?
How do you avoid leaking stack traces?
How do you correlate errors across services?
mistakes: Returning 200 with an error message.
Logging and swallowing exceptions.
interview: I want HTTP status to reflect the actual outcome. Centralized exception handling gives consistent client behavior and keeps controllers focused on business flow.
scenario: An endpoint catches an exception, logs it and returns a default response, so clients believe the operation succeeded.
investigation: Trace the exception path and inspect HTTP status mapping. Check whether global exception handling is bypassed by local catches.
resolution: Let unexpected exceptions propagate to a centralized exception handler and map them to appropriate status codes. Return a stable error contract with correlation information, not internal stack traces.
prevention: Define an error-response standard, test failure status codes and alert on unexpected 5xx rates rather than only application exceptions.

title: A memory leak appears after adding request caching
short: A cache without bounded cardinality is a memory leak from the application perspective even if every entry is technically reachable.
answer: I would confirm the retaining path with a heap dump, then inspect cache cardinality and eviction. The fix is to bound the cache and avoid storing large request objects, not simply increase heap size.
code: Bound the cache by size and TTL, store only the data required for reuse and avoid retaining request-scoped objects. If the data needs distributed durability, use an external cache with explicit eviction.
followups: How do you take a heap dump safely?
How do you distinguish a leak from normal heap growth?
What GC metrics would you monitor?
mistakes: Increasing heap size without finding the retaining object.
Using an unbounded map as a cache.
interview: I would use heap analysis to prove what is retaining memory, then bound the cache by size and lifetime.
scenario: Heap usage grows continuously in production even after traffic returns to normal. A new in-memory cache stores request-derived objects.
investigation: Use heap dumps and allocation profiling. Identify the retaining path and cache size, eviction policy and key cardinality. Check whether user/request objects are referenced longer than intended.
resolution: Bound the cache by size and TTL, store only the data required for reuse and avoid retaining request-scoped objects. If the data needs distributed durability, use an external cache with explicit eviction.
prevention: Monitor heap occupancy and cache cardinality, test long-running workloads and set memory alerts before the process reaches OOM.

title: Spring Security allows an endpoint that should be admin-only
short: Authentication proves identity; authorization decides whether that identity can perform the operation.
answer: I would verify the filter-chain rule and method-security configuration, then test the endpoint with users having different authorities. Authorization should be enforced server-side and covered by integration tests.
code: Define authorization at the correct layer and use explicit authorities/roles consistently. Add integration tests that assert both allowed and forbidden users receive the expected status.
followups: Role versus authority in Spring Security?
How do you test forbidden access?
mistakes: Checking permissions only in the frontend.
Mixing ROLE_ADMIN and ADMIN conventions.
interview: I would debug authorization from the token claims through the filter chain to the method decision, not just inspect the annotation.
scenario: An endpoint is protected by authentication, but any logged-in user can call it because the method-level role check was not applied as expected.
investigation: Inspect the filter chain, endpoint matchers, method-security configuration and exact authority names. Verify whether the call is going through a proxy and whether annotations are enabled.
resolution: Define authorization at the correct layer and use explicit authorities/roles consistently. Add integration tests that assert both allowed and forbidden users receive the expected status.
prevention: Treat authorization tests as security regression tests. Avoid relying on controller visibility or UI restrictions.

title: CPU usage spikes after switching to parallel streams
short: Parallel streams can increase throughput for suitable CPU-bound workloads, but they also consume shared executor capacity.
answer: I would profile CPU and common-pool contention first. If the workload is already concurrent or too small, sequential processing may be faster. For isolated batch work I would use a dedicated executor with controlled parallelism.
code: Remove parallelism if the workload is small or already concurrent. For controlled background workloads, use an appropriately sized executor instead of allowing common-pool work to compete with unrelated tasks.
followups: How does the common ForkJoinPool work?
How do virtual threads differ from parallel streams?
mistakes: Using parallel streams for blocking I/O.
Assuming more parallelism always means more throughput.
interview: I would not assume parallelStream is automatically faster. I would benchmark it and check whether it competes with other workloads for the common pool.
scenario: A batch endpoint uses parallelStream() and production CPU reaches 100%, while unrelated requests become slower.
investigation: Inspect ForkJoinPool activity, CPU profiles and request concurrency. Determine whether the work is CPU-bound and whether parallelism is competing with request threads.
resolution: Remove parallelism if the workload is small or already concurrent. For controlled background workloads, use an appropriately sized executor instead of allowing common-pool work to compete with unrelated tasks.
prevention: Benchmark realistic data sizes and concurrency. Treat the common ForkJoinPool as shared infrastructure rather than a free worker pool.

title: ThreadLocal data leaks between requests in a pooled executor
short: ThreadLocal is thread-scoped, not request-scoped; pooled threads survive after a request finishes.
answer: I would always clear ThreadLocal state in a finally block when using it with thread pools. For modern applications I would consider explicit context objects or framework-supported context propagation instead.
code: Use try/finally to remove ThreadLocal values, or prefer explicit context propagation mechanisms. Avoid storing large request objects in ThreadLocal.
followups: Why can ThreadLocal cause memory leaks?
How does this interact with virtual threads?
mistakes: Setting ThreadLocal without remove().
Assuming a pooled thread is destroyed after each request.
interview: ThreadLocal is safe only when its lifecycle matches the thread. In a pool, that means I must clean it after every task.
scenario: A request stores user context in ThreadLocal. A later request handled by the same pooled thread unexpectedly sees the previous request’s value.
investigation: Inspect where ThreadLocal is set and removed. Confirm thread reuse and whether exceptions can bypass cleanup.
resolution: Use try/finally to remove ThreadLocal values, or prefer explicit context propagation mechanisms. Avoid storing large request objects in ThreadLocal.
prevention: Add tests for thread reuse and monitor memory retention. Keep request context scoped and cleaned deterministically.

title: A synchronized section becomes a throughput bottleneck
short: Synchronization provides correctness but can serialize throughput when a hot shared lock protects too much work.
answer: I would profile lock contention, minimize the critical section and look for key-based partitioning. If the access pattern fits, ConcurrentHashMap or finer-grained synchronization can improve concurrency.
code: Reduce the critical section, use concurrent data structures where appropriate and partition state by key so independent operations do not share one lock. Do not replace synchronized with another lock without measuring.
mistakes: Removing synchronization without proving thread safety.
Holding a lock while performing remote I/O.
interview: The question is not whether synchronized is slow; it is whether the critical section creates unnecessary contention.
scenario: A high-throughput service synchronizes access to a shared map. As traffic increases, thread contention grows and throughput stops scaling.
investigation: Use thread dumps and profiling to measure monitor contention and time spent inside the critical section. Determine whether the shared state can be partitioned.
resolution: Reduce the critical section, use concurrent data structures where appropriate and partition state by key so independent operations do not share one lock. Do not replace synchronized with another lock without measuring.
prevention: Track lock contention and benchmark with realistic concurrency. Design shared state to minimize contention from the start.

title: GC pauses cause intermittent latency spikes
short: GC tuning starts with understanding allocation and pause behavior; collector flags are not a substitute for profiling.
answer: I would correlate p99 latency with GC events, then profile allocation and object lifetime. I would first reduce unnecessary allocation and only then tune collector and heap settings based on measured behavior.
code: Reduce unnecessary allocations, investigate object lifetime and choose/tune a collector appropriate to the latency and heap requirements. Avoid changing GC settings blindly.
followups: How do you identify allocation hotspots?
What is a memory leak versus high allocation rate?
mistakes: Increasing heap without analyzing pauses.
Changing collectors without baseline measurements.
interview: I would prove the latency correlation with GC logs and metrics before changing JVM flags.
scenario: A Java service has normal average latency but p99 latency spikes every few minutes. GC logs show long pauses during the same periods.
investigation: Correlate GC pause times with request latency, allocation rate, heap occupancy and old-generation collections. Inspect allocation hotspots with profiling.
resolution: Reduce unnecessary allocations, investigate object lifetime and choose/tune a collector appropriate to the latency and heap requirements. Avoid changing GC settings blindly.
prevention: Track pause time, allocation rate, heap occupancy and p99 latency together. Load-test with production-like object allocation patterns.

title: A CompletableFuture chain silently stops after an exception
short: CompletableFuture exceptions complete the future exceptionally; they do not automatically behave like synchronous exceptions.
answer: I would inspect the chain for exceptional completion and ensure the final future is observed. I would use handle or exceptionally for recovery and whenComplete for cleanup, while preserving the failure when recovery is not possible.
code: Make exceptional paths explicit and return a terminal future that callers can observe. Use handle or exceptionally for recovery and whenComplete for side-effect cleanup/logging.
followups: What happens when an executor rejects a task?
How do you cancel a future chain?
mistakes: Assuming try/catch around submit catches async exceptions.
Ignoring the final future.
interview: Async errors live in the future. If nobody observes the final stage, the business failure can become invisible.
scenario: A multi-step asynchronous workflow produces no final result for some requests. Logs show an exception in an intermediate stage but no response handling.
investigation: Inspect the future chain and exceptional completion paths. Check whether exceptionally/handle/whenComplete is used and whether the final future is awaited.
resolution: Make exceptional paths explicit and return a terminal future that callers can observe. Use handle or exceptionally for recovery and whenComplete for side-effect cleanup/logging.
prevention: Test both success and failure paths for every asynchronous workflow and propagate correlation IDs through async boundaries.

title: A query becomes slow after the table grows tenfold
short: Query performance is data-dependent; an index that worked at small scale may become ineffective as selectivity and distribution change.
answer: I would compare execution plans and cardinality estimates first. Then I would tune indexes or query shape, update statistics and consider partitioning or archival only if the data model and access pattern justify it.
code: Choose indexes based on the actual predicates and ordering, update statistics and reduce unnecessary rows/columns. If the workload has outgrown one table, consider partitioning or archival based on access patterns.
followups: When can an optimizer ignore an index?
mistakes: Adding indexes without checking write cost.
Optimizing only against a tiny test dataset.
interview: I would not tune SQL from the text alone. I need the execution plan and realistic data distribution.
scenario: A query that was fast with 2 million rows becomes slow at 20 million rows even though the SQL text has not changed.
investigation: Compare execution plans before and after growth. Inspect row estimates, index usage, scan type, selectivity, sort/hash operations and returned row counts.
resolution: Choose indexes based on the actual predicates and ordering, update statistics and reduce unnecessary rows/columns. If the workload has outgrown one table, consider partitioning or archival based on access patterns.
prevention: Monitor plan regressions, index usage and data growth. Include representative data volume in performance testing.

title: A deadlock appears after a new transaction flow is deployed
short: Deadlocks usually come from inconsistent lock ordering combined with concurrency.
answer: I would inspect the deadlock graph, identify the lock order and make the transaction paths acquire resources consistently. I would also keep transactions short and use bounded retry only when the business operation is safe to repeat.
code: Make transactions acquire shared resources in a consistent order, keep transactions short and avoid unnecessary locks. Add safe retry for deadlock victims when the operation is idempotent and the database recommends it.
followups: How do isolation levels affect locking?
mistakes: Increasing lock timeouts.
Retrying non-idempotent operations blindly.
interview: I would fix the lock-ordering design first and use retry only as a resilience measure, not the primary solution.
scenario: Two transactions update the same business entities in different orders. Under concurrency, each waits for a lock held by the other.
investigation: Capture deadlock graphs or database diagnostics. Identify the resources and lock acquisition order for each transaction.
resolution: Make transactions acquire shared resources in a consistent order, keep transactions short and avoid unnecessary locks. Add safe retry for deadlock victims when the operation is idempotent and the database recommends it.
prevention: Test concurrent access patterns, monitor deadlock frequency and document lock ordering for critical workflows.

title: An index exists but the query still performs a full scan
short: Having an index is not enough; the predicate must allow the optimizer to use it efficiently.
answer: I would inspect the plan and predicate. If a function wraps the indexed column, I would usually rewrite it as a range predicate so the database can use the index, then verify with EXPLAIN.
code: Rewrite predicates into sargable ranges where possible, for example a half-open timestamp interval. Use functional indexes only when supported and justified by workload.
followups: When is a functional index useful?
Why can a selective index still be ignored?
mistakes: Assuming every WHERE clause can use the index.
Applying functions to indexed columns unnecessarily.
interview: I would validate index usability through the execution plan, not by checking that the index exists.
scenario: A query filters on a timestamp column with a function applied to it. An index exists, but the optimizer chooses a full table scan.
investigation: Inspect the predicate and execution plan. Check whether the expression prevents efficient index range access and whether selectivity is sufficient.
resolution: Rewrite predicates into sargable ranges where possible, for example a half-open timestamp interval. Use functional indexes only when supported and justified by workload.
prevention: Review common predicates during index design and test with production-like statistics.

title: A large delete locks the table and causes API timeouts
short: Large maintenance transactions can create operational incidents even when the SQL is logically correct.
answer: I would avoid one giant transaction. I would batch the deletion, control commit frequency and consider partition-based retention if the data is naturally time-partitioned.
code: Delete in bounded batches, commit between batches when business rules allow and schedule heavy maintenance during lower traffic. For very large time-based data, partitioning can make retention operations cheaper.
followups: When should batching not be used?
How does partition dropping help retention?
What are the consistency implications of batch deletes?
mistakes: Deleting millions of rows in one transaction.
Ignoring transaction-log and replication impact.
interview: For large data operations I care about lock duration, log volume and impact on foreground traffic, not only total execution time.
scenario: A maintenance job deletes millions of old rows in one transaction. Application requests start timing out because of lock and I/O pressure.
investigation: Inspect transaction duration, lock waits, log growth and database I/O. Determine whether the delete conflicts with active queries.
resolution: Delete in bounded batches, commit between batches when business rules allow and schedule heavy maintenance during lower traffic. For very large time-based data, partitioning can make retention operations cheaper.
prevention: Load-test maintenance jobs against production-like traffic and monitor lock duration and transaction log growth.

title: Pagination becomes slower on deep pages
short: OFFSET pagination makes the database walk past rows that are not returned; keyset pagination starts from the last seen key.
answer: For very deep pages I would replace OFFSET with keyset pagination using an indexed, deterministic sort key such as created_at plus a unique ID. This keeps work closer to the requested page size.
code: Use keyset/seek pagination based on a stable indexed ordering for large datasets. Keep cursor semantics explicit and avoid exposing mutable offset-based navigation when consistent traversal matters.
followups: How do you paginate with duplicate timestamps?
mistakes: Using only created_at when timestamps are not unique.
Treating a cursor as a random page number.
interview: I would use offset pagination for simple shallow navigation and keyset pagination for large, high-volume feeds.
scenario: An API uses OFFSET 5,000,000 LIMIT 50. The first pages are fast, but deep pages become increasingly slow.
investigation: Inspect the execution plan and amount of rows scanned/discarded before the requested page. Measure latency as offset grows.
resolution: Use keyset/seek pagination based on a stable indexed ordering for large datasets. Keep cursor semantics explicit and avoid exposing mutable offset-based navigation when consistent traversal matters.
prevention: Index the cursor columns, define deterministic ordering and test pagination at realistic data volume.

title: JWT validation passes but a user accesses another user’s resource
short: A valid JWT proves who the caller is; it does not automatically prove they may access every resource.
answer: I would keep JWT validation and resource authorization separate. The service must compare the authenticated subject and tenant context with the resource owner or permission model before returning data.
code: Separate authentication from authorization. Enforce object-level authorization using the authenticated subject, tenant and resource ownership/permissions. Never treat a valid token as permission to every resource.
followups: How do you implement tenant-aware authorization?
Should authorization be checked at the gateway?
mistakes: Assuming authentication implies authorization.
Trusting user IDs from the URL without authorization checks.
interview: The classic JWT mistake is treating authentication as authorization. I would explicitly authorize the requested object for the authenticated principal.
scenario: The API validates the JWT correctly, but a user can change /users/123 to /users/124 and retrieve another user’s data.
investigation: Confirm token validation and then inspect the authorization decision for the requested resource. Check whether the resource owner is compared with token claims or server-side permissions.
resolution: Separate authentication from authorization. Enforce object-level authorization using the authenticated subject, tenant and resource ownership/permissions. Never treat a valid token as permission to every resource.
prevention: Add authorization tests for horizontal privilege escalation and audit access to sensitive resources.

title: Refresh-token rotation causes unexpected logouts
short: Refresh-token rotation improves security, but token state must be modeled per session when multiple devices are supported.
answer: I would model refresh tokens as session-specific token families. Each refresh rotates the token and invalidates the predecessor. Reuse of an old token can indicate theft and should revoke that token family.
code: Track refresh-token families per device/session. Rotate the token on refresh, invalidate the old token, and detect reuse. Do not store one refresh token as the only session state for a multi-device account unless that behavior is intentional.
followups: How do you revoke JWT access tokens?
What happens if two refresh requests race?
Where should refresh tokens be stored?
mistakes: Keeping one refresh token per user for all devices.
Rotating without handling concurrent refreshes.
interview: I would first clarify whether sessions are per device. Then I would use token-family rotation and reuse detection rather than one global refresh token.
scenario: A user signs in on two devices. Refresh-token rotation is enabled, but refreshing on one device invalidates the other device’s session unexpectedly.
investigation: Inspect whether refresh tokens are rotated per session, globally per user, or stored as a single token. Check token-family tracking and reuse detection.
resolution: Track refresh-token families per device/session. Rotate the token on refresh, invalidate the old token, and detect reuse. Do not store one refresh token as the only session state for a multi-device account unless that behavior is intentional.
prevention: Define session semantics, expose device/session management and test concurrent refreshes and token theft scenarios.

title: An SSRF vulnerability lets the backend call internal services
short: SSRF is a server-side trust-boundary problem: user-controlled URLs become server-controlled network requests.
answer: I would avoid arbitrary outbound URLs where possible. If required, I would use an allowlist, validate DNS-resolved addresses against blocked ranges, restrict redirects and enforce network egress controls.
code: Prefer allowlists for destinations. Validate resolved IP addresses, block private/link-local/loopback ranges, control redirects and use an egress proxy where appropriate. Do not rely only on string checks of the hostname.
followups: Which cloud metadata endpoints are sensitive?
mistakes: Blocking only localhost strings.
Allowing redirects to bypass validation.
interview: The strongest SSRF defense is reducing where the server is allowed to connect, not only validating the input string.
scenario: An image-import endpoint accepts a URL and fetches it from the server. An attacker supplies an internal metadata or service address.
investigation: Trace outbound URL handling and inspect whether private IPs, loopback addresses, redirects and DNS rebinding are blocked. Identify whether the server follows redirects automatically.
resolution: Prefer allowlists for destinations. Validate resolved IP addresses, block private/link-local/loopback ranges, control redirects and use an egress proxy where appropriate. Do not rely only on string checks of the hostname.
prevention: Add SSRF tests, restrict outbound network access and monitor unusual outbound destinations.

title: Kubernetes repeatedly OOMKills a Java service
short: Container memory is larger than Java heap; the process can be OOMKilled while heap is not full.
answer: I would compare container RSS with heap usage and account for metaspace, thread stacks, direct memory and native allocations. Then I would fix leaks or allocation pressure and size the JVM with explicit headroom inside the container limit.
code: Size JVM memory within the container limit, leaving headroom for non-heap/native memory. Investigate allocation or leaks before simply increasing the container limit. Set realistic requests/limits and test peak load.
followups: How does -Xmx relate to container limits?
How do you investigate native memory?
What is the difference between requests and limits?
mistakes: Setting Xmx equal to the container memory limit.
Assuming OOMKilled always means a Java heap leak.
interview: I would never infer container safety from heap usage alone. Kubernetes limits apply to the whole process.
scenario: A Java pod is stable under normal traffic but gets OOMKilled during peak load. The JVM heap appears below the configured heap maximum shortly before termination.
investigation: Compare container memory limit with JVM heap plus metaspace, thread stacks, native memory, direct buffers and other process overhead. Inspect container memory metrics and JVM native-memory data.
resolution: Size JVM memory within the container limit, leaving headroom for non-heap/native memory. Investigate allocation or leaks before simply increasing the container limit. Set realistic requests/limits and test peak load.
prevention: Monitor container RSS and JVM heap separately, alert before the limit and include container limits in JVM sizing decisions.

title: A rolling deployment causes capacity to drop below the SLO
short: Zero-downtime deployment depends on capacity, readiness and rollout policy together.
answer: I would ensure the rollout maintains enough ready capacity, usually with maxUnavailable set appropriately and maxSurge supported by cluster capacity. Readiness must prevent traffic from reaching unready pods.
code: Use readiness probes that reflect serving capability and configure rollout capacity so enough replicas remain available. For critical services, use maxUnavailable=0 where capacity permits and ensure cluster resources can support surge pods.
followups: How do readiness probes interact with deployments?
mistakes: Assuming rolling updates are automatically zero downtime.
Ignoring cluster capacity for surge pods.
interview: I would test deployments as production traffic events, not just application tests.
scenario: A service runs four pods. During rolling deployment, one old pod is terminated before a new pod becomes ready, leaving only three serving instances and causing latency spikes.
investigation: Inspect deployment strategy, maxUnavailable, maxSurge and readiness behavior. Compare available replicas with traffic and per-pod capacity.
resolution: Use readiness probes that reflect serving capability and configure rollout capacity so enough replicas remain available. For critical services, use maxUnavailable=0 where capacity permits and ensure cluster resources can support surge pods.
prevention: Load-test rollouts, monitor available replicas and latency during deployments and ensure the cluster has spare capacity for surge.

title: A Kubernetes HPA scales too late during traffic spikes
short: Autoscaling is constrained by detection time plus pod startup time; the metric must predict saturation early enough.
answer: I would measure the complete scaling loop. If CPU is delayed, I would consider request concurrency or queue depth, increase baseline capacity for known peaks and optimize pod startup time.
code: Use a metric that correlates earlier with saturation, such as request rate, concurrency or queue depth, and tune target utilization and startup capacity. Keep a minimum replica buffer for predictable peaks.
followups: When is queue depth a better metric?
How does cluster autoscaler interact with HPA?
mistakes: Choosing CPU because it is easy to measure.
Ignoring pod startup latency.
interview: I would tune autoscaling from the service’s actual bottleneck and response time, not blindly use CPU at 70 percent.
scenario: Traffic doubles in 30 seconds, but CPU-based HPA takes several minutes to add enough pods. p95 latency breaches the SLO before scaling completes.
investigation: Measure scale-up detection delay, pod startup time and whether CPU is a leading indicator for this workload. Check stabilization and metrics scrape intervals.
resolution: Use a metric that correlates earlier with saturation, such as request rate, concurrency or queue depth, and tune target utilization and startup capacity. Keep a minimum replica buffer for predictable peaks.
prevention: Load-test burst traffic, measure time-to-ready and set alerts on saturation before the SLO is breached.

title: Design an order system that remains correct during duplicate requests
short: Correctness comes from durable idempotency and explicit state transitions, not from assuming requests arrive once.
answer: I would design order creation around an idempotency key and durable order state. The payment flow would have its own idempotency and reconciliation because an external timeout does not prove failure.
code: Create an idempotent order command keyed by a client-generated idempotency key. Persist the key and order result atomically. Use a payment provider idempotency key derived from the order attempt and model payment as a state machine with reconciliation.
followups: How would you scale the order database?
How would you publish OrderCreated reliably?
What if payment remains pending for 30 minutes?
mistakes: Treating order creation and payment as one synchronous ACID transaction.
Ignoring duplicate client requests.
interview: I would first define the business state machine and failure semantics, then design APIs and storage around those guarantees.
scenario: Customers can retry order creation because mobile networks are unreliable. The system must not create duplicate orders or double-charge customers.
investigation: Identify the command boundary, idempotency key, order state machine and payment interaction. Separate order creation from payment outcome and model uncertain states.
resolution: Create an idempotent order command keyed by a client-generated idempotency key. Persist the key and order result atomically. Use a payment provider idempotency key derived from the order attempt and model payment as a state machine with reconciliation.
prevention: Test retries, concurrent duplicates, provider timeouts and partial failures. Store durable correlation IDs and expose safe status queries.

title: Design a notification service for millions of users
short: The API should not synchronously wait for external notification providers at scale.
answer: I would make notification submission asynchronous. The API writes a durable command, channel workers consume it, apply provider-specific rate limits and retries, and persist delivery status for observability and reconciliation.
code: Accept notification commands into a durable queue, route by channel, use provider-specific workers and bounded retries with backoff. Track delivery state and use idempotency keys to prevent duplicate sends where the provider supports them.
followups: How do you preserve ordering for notifications?
How do you handle provider rate limits?
How do you prevent duplicate SMS?
mistakes: Retrying without provider rate limits.
Using one shared worker pool for all channels.
interview: I would separate acceptance from delivery so provider slowness does not directly make the public API unavailable.
scenario: A platform sends email, SMS and push notifications. Traffic is bursty and a provider may become slow or unavailable.
investigation: Estimate peak notification rate, provider quotas, queue capacity and retry volume. Separate request acceptance from delivery execution.
resolution: Accept notification commands into a durable queue, route by channel, use provider-specific workers and bounded retries with backoff. Track delivery state and use idempotency keys to prevent duplicate sends where the provider supports them.
prevention: Monitor queue age, provider latency, delivery success and retry rates. Apply per-provider rate limits and circuit breakers.

title: Design a distributed rate limiter for APIs
short: A distributed rate limiter is a consistency and availability trade-off, not just a counter.
answer: I would use a token bucket or sliding-window approach with atomic state updates in a shared store. I would define the failure policy explicitly and expose rate-limit headers so clients can behave predictably.
code: Use a centralized or distributed counter/token-bucket implementation with atomic operations. Return 429 with retry guidance. Decide whether fail-open or fail-closed is safer for the business operation.
followups: How do you avoid a Redis bottleneck?
What happens during a Redis outage?
mistakes: Using local counters when the limit must be global.
Ignoring burst behavior.
interview: I would first clarify the accuracy requirement. Then I would choose token bucket or sliding window, atomic updates and an explicit fail-open/fail-closed policy.
scenario: A public API must enforce 100 requests per minute per customer across many application instances.
investigation: Define whether the limit is strict or approximate, the key dimensions and failure behavior. Estimate request volume and state size. Decide whether the limiter must be globally consistent.
resolution: Use a centralized or distributed counter/token-bucket implementation with atomic operations. Return 429 with retry guidance. Decide whether fail-open or fail-closed is safer for the business operation.
prevention: Monitor allowed/blocked rates and limiter latency, protect the limiter itself and load-test bursts at the boundary.

title: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters
short: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated characters.
answer: Use a sliding window. Keep the last index of every character in a HashMap. When a repeated character is found inside the current window, move the left boundary to one position after its previous index.
followups: What changes if the input is Unicode?
Can you return the substring instead of its length?
mistakes: Do not move the left pointer backwards.
A Set-only solution can work, but the map gives a clean O(n) implementation.
interview: I use a sliding window with a map of each character's latest index. When a duplicate appears, I move the left pointer past the previous occurrence. Each character is processed once, giving O(n) time.
problem: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated characters.
example:
Input: "abcabcbb"
Output: 3
Explanation: "abc" is the longest substring without repeating characters.
approach: Use a sliding window. Keep the last index of every character in a HashMap. When a repeated character is found inside the current window, move the left boundary to one position after its previous index.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(min(n, character-set-size))

title: Maximum subarray sum using Kadane’s algorithm
short: Find the contiguous subarray with the maximum sum and return that sum.
answer: Maintain the best sum ending at the current position. At each element, either start a new subarray with that element or extend the previous subarray. Track the maximum seen globally.
followups: How would you return the actual subarray?
How do you handle an empty array?
mistakes: Do not initialize the running sum to zero if all-negative arrays must be handled correctly.
interview: I keep two values: the best sum ending at the current index and the best sum seen overall. For each number I decide whether extending the previous subarray is better than starting fresh. This is Kadane’s algorithm with O(n) time and O(1) space.
problem: Find the contiguous subarray with the maximum sum and return that sum.
approach: Maintain the best sum ending at the current position. At each element, either start a new subarray with that element or extend the previous subarray. Track the maximum seen globally.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)

title: Rotate an array to the right by k positions
short: Rotate an integer array to the right by k positions in-place.
answer: Normalize k using k % n. Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements and the remaining elements. This achieves rotation in-place without an auxiliary array.
followups: What if k is larger than the array length?
Can you do it with an extra array?
mistakes: Forgetting k %= n causes unnecessary work and edge-case errors.
interview: I normalize k and use the three-reversal technique: reverse the entire array, reverse the first k elements, then reverse the rest. It gives O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
problem: Rotate an integer array to the right by k positions in-place.
approach: Normalize k using k % n. Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements and the remaining elements. This achieves rotation in-place without an auxiliary array.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)

title: Merge overlapping intervals
short: Given intervals, merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping result.
answer: Sort intervals by start time. Maintain the current interval. If the next start is within the current end, extend the current end; otherwise add the current interval and start a new one.
followups: How would you insert one new interval into an already merged list?
mistakes: Do not compare only the next end; the merged end must use Math.max.
interview: I sort by interval start and then scan once. Overlapping intervals are merged by extending the current end. Sorting dominates the complexity at O(n log n).
problem: Given intervals, merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping result.
approach: Sort intervals by start time. Maintain the current interval. If the next start is within the current end, extend the current end; otherwise add the current interval and start a new one.
complexity:
Time: O(n log n)
Space: O(n) for the result

title: Product of array except self
short: For each position, return the product of every other element without using division.
answer: Store prefix products in the output array. Then scan from right to left while maintaining a suffix product and multiply it into each output position. This also handles zeros without special cases.
followups: What happens with one or more zeros?
Can you prove why two passes are sufficient?
mistakes: Do not use an additional prefix and suffix array if O(1) extra space is expected.
interview: I build prefix products into the result and then multiply each position by the suffix product in a reverse pass. No division is required, and zero values are naturally handled.
problem: For each position, return the product of every other element without using division.
approach: Store prefix products in the output array. Then scan from right to left while maintaining a suffix product and multiply it into each output position. This also handles zeros without special cases.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1) extra, excluding the output array

title: Find all unique triplets that sum to zero
short: Given an integer array, return all unique triplets whose values sum to zero.
answer: Sort the array. Fix one element and use two pointers for the remaining range. Skip duplicate values at the fixed pointer and after a match so that the result contains unique triplets.
mistakes: Skipping duplicates is essential.
Use long for the sum when integer overflow is possible.
interview: I sort first, then for each fixed value use two pointers. Sorting lets me move the pointers based on the sum and also makes duplicate skipping straightforward. The overall time is O(n²).
problem: Given an integer array, return all unique triplets whose values sum to zero.
approach: Sort the array. Fix one element and use two pointers for the remaining range. Skip duplicate values at the fixed pointer and after a match so that the result contains unique triplets.
complexity:
Time: O(n^2)
Space: O(n) for the output; O(1) auxiliary apart from sorting implementation

title: Find the first and last position of a target in a sorted array
short: Return the first and last index of a target value in a sorted array. If absent, return [-1,-1].
answer: Run binary search twice: once biased toward the left to find the first occurrence and once biased toward the right to find the last occurrence.
followups: Can you find the insertion range?
What changes if the array is descending?
mistakes: Do not return immediately after finding the target.
interview: I use two modified binary searches. When I find the target, I record the index and continue left for the first occurrence or right for the last. This keeps the complexity at O(log n).
problem: Return the first and last index of a target value in a sorted array. If absent, return [-1,-1].
approach: Run binary search twice: once biased toward the left to find the first occurrence and once biased toward the right to find the last occurrence.
complexity:
Time: O(log n)
Space: O(1)

title: Find the kth largest element using a min-heap
short: Find the kth largest element without fully sorting the array.
answer: Maintain a min-heap of size k. Add every value; when the heap exceeds k, remove its smallest value. At the end, the root is the kth largest.
followups: How can Quickselect improve average complexity?
How would you find the kth smallest?
mistakes: A max-heap is less convenient for kth largest in this approach.
interview: A min-heap of size k keeps only the k largest elements seen so far. The smallest of those k values is the kth largest overall.
problem: Find the kth largest element without fully sorting the array.
approach: Maintain a min-heap of size k. Add every value; when the heap exceeds k, remove its smallest value. At the end, the root is the kth largest.
complexity:
Time: O(n log k)
Space: O(k)

title: Merge k sorted linked lists
short: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list.
answer: Put the head of every non-empty list into a min-heap. Repeatedly remove the smallest node, append it to the result, and add its next node.
followups: What if k is extremely large?
mistakes: Heap size is k, not N.
interview: I keep one candidate node from each list in a min-heap. Every extraction gives the next smallest value, and I insert that node’s successor. This is O(N log k).
problem: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list.
example:
Input: 3 sorted lists such as [1,4,5], [1,3,4], [2,6]
Output: [1,1,2,3,4,4,5,6]
approach: Put the head of every non-empty list into a min-heap. Repeatedly remove the smallest node, append it to the result, and add its next node.
complexity:
Time: O(N log k)
Space: O(k)

title: Reverse a singly linked list
short: Reverse a singly linked list iteratively.
answer: Maintain previous and current pointers. Save current.next, reverse the pointer to previous, then advance both pointers.
followups: How do you reverse nodes in groups of k?
mistakes: Save next before changing current.next.
interview: I reverse one pointer at a time using prev and current references. I save the next node before changing the current link so I never lose the remainder of the list.
problem: Reverse a singly linked list iteratively.
approach: Maintain previous and current pointers. Save current.next, reverse the pointer to previous, then advance both pointers.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)

title: Check whether a linked list is a palindrome
short: Determine whether the values in a singly linked list form a palindrome.
answer: Use slow and fast pointers to find the midpoint, reverse the second half, then compare the first and second halves. Optionally restore the list afterward.
followups: Would you restore the list after checking?
Can you solve it with a stack?
mistakes: Be careful with odd-length lists; the fast pointer naturally handles the middle element.
interview: I find the midpoint with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, and compare both halves. This avoids allocating an array and uses O(1) auxiliary space.
problem: Determine whether the values in a singly linked list form a palindrome.
approach: Use slow and fast pointers to find the midpoint, reverse the second half, then compare the first and second halves. Optionally restore the list afterward.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1) auxiliary

title: Find the maximum depth of a binary tree
short: Return the maximum number of nodes along a root-to-leaf path.
answer: The depth of a node is one plus the maximum depth of its children. Use recursion for a concise solution; an iterative BFS solution is also possible.
followups: How would you implement it iteratively?
What happens for a skewed tree?
mistakes: Tree height determines recursion depth.
interview: For every node, I calculate one plus the maximum depth of the left and right subtrees. Every node is visited once.
problem: Return the maximum number of nodes along a root-to-leaf path.
approach: The depth of a node is one plus the maximum depth of its children. Use recursion for a concise solution; an iterative BFS solution is also possible.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(h) recursion stack

title: Level-order traversal of a binary tree
short: Return the values of a binary tree level by level.
answer: Use a queue for breadth-first traversal. At each iteration capture the current queue size; those nodes belong to one level.
followups: How would you do zigzag traversal?
mistakes: Do not iterate over a changing queue size without capturing the level size first.
interview: I use a queue to process nodes breadth-first. The queue size at the start of each iteration tells me exactly how many nodes belong to that level.
problem: Return the values of a binary tree level by level.
approach: Use a queue for breadth-first traversal. At each iteration capture the current queue size; those nodes belong to one level.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(w), where w is maximum tree width

title: Validate whether a binary tree is a binary search tree
short: Determine whether a binary tree satisfies the BST ordering rule for every node.
answer: Pass a valid numeric range down the tree. Every left child must be below the current upper bound and every right child above the current lower bound.
followups: How do duplicates change the rule?
Can you solve it with inorder traversal?
mistakes: Checking only parent-child relationships is insufficient.
interview: I validate the entire allowed range for every node instead of checking only its immediate children. That catches violations deeper in the tree.
problem: Determine whether a binary tree satisfies the BST ordering rule for every node.
approach: Pass a valid numeric range down the tree. Every left child must be below the current upper bound and every right child above the current lower bound.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(h)

title: Lowest common ancestor in a binary search tree
short: Find the lowest node in a BST that has two given values in its subtree.
answer: If both targets are smaller, move left. If both are larger, move right. Otherwise the current node is where their paths split and is the LCA.
followups: How does LCA change for a normal binary tree?
What if one target is not present?
mistakes: The BST optimization depends on the ordering invariant.
interview: Because it is a BST, I can use ordering to walk only one path. When the two target values fall on different sides of the current node, that node is their lowest common ancestor.
problem: Find the lowest node in a BST that has two given values in its subtree.
approach: If both targets are smaller, move left. If both are larger, move right. Otherwise the current node is where their paths split and is the LCA.
complexity:
Time: O(h)
Space: O(1)

title: Implement a Trie for word insertion and lookup
short: Implement a Trie supporting insert and exact word search.
answer: Each Trie node has a map of outgoing characters and an end-of-word flag. Insertion walks or creates one node per character; search follows the same path and checks the final flag.
followups: How would you implement prefix search?
How would you reduce memory for a fixed alphabet?
mistakes: The end flag distinguishes "car" from the prefix "ca".
interview: A Trie stores characters as a tree. The key interview point is that lookup time depends on word length rather than the number of stored words, assuming hash-map child lookup.
problem: Implement a Trie supporting insert and exact word search.
example: Operations: insert("cat"), insert("car"), search("cat") -> true, search("can") -> false
approach: Each Trie node has a map of outgoing characters and an end-of-word flag. Insertion walks or creates one node per character; search follows the same path and checks the final flag.
complexity:
Time: O(L) per operation
Space: O(total characters stored)

title: Count islands in a binary grid
short: Count connected groups of 1s in a grid where horizontal and vertical neighbors belong to the same island.
answer: Scan every cell. When an unvisited land cell is found, increment the count and flood-fill its island using BFS or DFS, marking visited cells so the island is not counted again.
followups: Can you solve it with Union-Find?
mistakes: Mark cells when enqueuing, not when dequeuing, to avoid duplicate queue entries.
interview: I treat each unvisited land cell as the start of a BFS flood-fill. The BFS marks the complete island, so every grid cell is processed at most once.
problem: Count connected groups of 1s in a grid where horizontal and vertical neighbors belong to the same island.
approach: Scan every cell. When an unvisited land cell is found, increment the count and flood-fill its island using BFS or DFS, marking visited cells so the island is not counted again.
complexity:
Time: O(rows * cols)
Space: O(rows * cols) worst case for the queue

title: Shortest path in a grid using BFS
short: Find the minimum number of moves from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell in a grid where 0 is open and 1 is blocked.
answer: Because every move has equal cost, BFS explores cells in increasing distance order. Store the distance with each queue entry and stop when the destination is reached.
followups: When would Dijkstra be needed instead?
How would you return the actual path?
mistakes: DFS does not guarantee the shortest path in an unweighted grid.
interview: BFS is appropriate because every move costs the same. The first time I reach the destination, I have found the shortest path length.
problem: Find the minimum number of moves from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell in a grid where 0 is open and 1 is blocked.
approach: Because every move has equal cost, BFS explores cells in increasing distance order. Store the distance with each queue entry and stop when the destination is reached.
complexity:
Time: O(rows * cols)
Space: O(rows * cols)

title: Coin change: minimum number of coins
short: Given coin denominations and a target amount, find the minimum number of coins required to make that amount.
answer: Use bottom-up dynamic programming. dp[a] is the minimum coins needed for amount a. For each amount, try every coin and use dp[a-coin] + 1.
followups: Why does greedy not always work?
Can you solve it top-down with memoization?
mistakes: Initialize unreachable states to a value larger than any possible answer.
interview: I define dp[a] as the minimum number of coins for amount a. Every coin gives a transition from a smaller amount, so bottom-up DP computes the answer without recomputing subproblems.
problem: Given coin denominations and a target amount, find the minimum number of coins required to make that amount.
approach: Use bottom-up dynamic programming. dp[a] is the minimum coins needed for amount a. For each amount, try every coin and use dp[a-coin] + 1.
complexity:
Time: O(amount * numberOfCoins)
Space: O(amount)

title: Climbing stairs with dynamic programming
short: Count the number of distinct ways to reach the nth stair when you can climb either 1 or 2 steps at a time.
answer: The number of ways to reach n equals ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). Keep only the previous two values because older values are no longer needed.
followups: What if you can climb 1, 2 or 3 steps?
What happens for large n and integer overflow?
mistakes: Clarify whether n=0 should return 1 or 0 based on the problem definition.
interview: This is Fibonacci-like DP. The current number of ways is the sum of the ways to reach the previous two stairs, and only those two values need to be retained.
problem: Count the number of distinct ways to reach the nth stair when you can climb either 1 or 2 steps at a time.
approach: The number of ways to reach n equals ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). Keep only the previous two values because older values are no longer needed.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)

title: Group employees by department using Java Streams
short: Given employees, group them by department and print each department with its employees.
answer: Use Collectors.groupingBy with the department as the classifier. The result is a Map from department to a list of employees.
followups: How would you count employees instead of storing them?
How would you find the highest-paid employee per department?
mistakes: Do not confuse groupingBy with partitioningBy; partitioning is for a boolean predicate.
interview: I use groupingBy with the department as the classifier. This is preferable to manually maintaining maps because the collector expresses the grouping intent directly.
problem: Given employees, group them by department and print each department with its employees.
example:
Input: Arun-IT, Bala-HR, Ravi-IT
Output: IT -> [Arun,Ravi], HR -> [Bala]
approach: Use Collectors.groupingBy with the department as the classifier. The result is a Map from department to a list of employees.
complexity:
Time: O(n) expected for grouping
Space: O(n) for the grouped result

title: Partition numbers into even and odd using Streams
short: Partition a list of integers into even and odd numbers using Java Streams.
answer: Use Collectors.partitioningBy with a predicate that checks whether a number is even. The result always has boolean keys for the two partitions.
followups: How is partitioningBy different from groupingBy?
mistakes: partitioningBy uses a boolean classifier; groupingBy can classify into arbitrary keys.
interview: partitioningBy is the natural collector when the classification is a boolean predicate. It produces the two groups without manually creating two lists.
problem: Partition a list of integers into even and odd numbers using Java Streams.
approach: Use Collectors.partitioningBy with a predicate that checks whether a number is even. The result always has boolean keys for the two partitions.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n) for the output

title: Find the top 3 highest-paid employees using Streams
short: Return the top three employees by salary in descending order.
answer: Stream the employees, sort by salary descending, limit to three, and collect the result. For large data sets, discuss database-side sorting when the data originates in a database.
followups: How would you find the top 3 per department?
Can you use a priority queue for better memory behavior?
mistakes: Mention the database-side alternative for production-sized data.
interview: I sort by salary descending and take the first three. In a backend application backed by a database, I would normally push this ordering and limit into SQL rather than loading all employees into memory.
problem: Return the top three employees by salary in descending order.
example:
Employees: Arun 70000, Ravi 90000, Priya 80000, Anand 95000
Output: Anand, Ravi, Priya
approach: Stream the employees, sort by salary descending, limit to three, and collect the result. For large data sets, discuss database-side sorting when the data originates in a database.
complexity:
Time: O(n log n) due to sorting
Space: O(n) depending on stream sorting

title: Find duplicate numbers in an array using Streams
short: Find all values that occur more than once in an integer array using Java Streams.
answer: Maintain a Set of values already seen. In the stream filter, a value is a duplicate when add(value) returns false. Collect the duplicates into a distinct result.
followups: Is this approach safe with parallel streams?
How would you return frequency counts instead?
mistakes: Avoid shared mutable state in parallel streams; this particular technique is intended for sequential processing.
interview: The important idea is that HashSet.add returns false when the value already exists. That lets the stream identify duplicates in one pass while a second set preserves unique duplicate values.
problem: Find all values that occur more than once in an integer array using Java Streams.
approach: Maintain a Set of values already seen. In the stream filter, a value is a duplicate when add(value) returns false. Collect the duplicates into a distinct result.
complexity:
Time: O(n) expected
Space: O(n)

title: Order API creates duplicate orders after client retries
short: Idempotency makes a retried business operation produce the same logical result rather than creating another order.
answer: The important distinction is between transport retries and business retries. A timeout does not mean the server did not commit. I would use an idempotency key persisted with a unique constraint, make the create operation atomic, and propagate the idempotency key to payment.
followups: How would you expire idempotency keys?
What if the first request is still processing when the retry arrives?
mistakes: Do not implement check-then-insert without a database uniqueness guarantee.
interview: I would first prove whether the duplicate originates in the API, message layer, or payment provider. Then I would enforce uniqueness at the database boundary instead of relying only on application checks.
scenario: Mobile clients retry POST /orders when the network times out. Customers occasionally see two orders and two downstream payment attempts.
investigation: Trace one duplicated request using a correlation ID and inspect whether the same idempotency key was supplied. Check database uniqueness constraints, payment calls, retry behavior and whether the response was lost after the first commit.
prevention: Require a client-generated idempotency key. Persist the key with the order in a unique-constrained table, make the operation transactional, and return the original result for a repeated key. Make payment initiation idempotent as well.
