title: Kafka consumers fall behind during peak traffic
short: Consumer lag means the group is not processing records as quickly as they arrive. The fix depends on whether the bottleneck is Kafka, consumer compute, partitions or downstream I/O.
answer: I would compare producer throughput with consumer throughput first. Then I would inspect partition distribution, rebalance frequency and consumer processing time. If the consumer is healthy but under-provisioned, I can scale it up to the partition count; if processing is slow, I fix the downstream bottleneck instead of blindly adding consumers.
followups: Why can adding consumers fail to improve lag?
How do you handle a poison message?
mistakes: Do not assume CPU is the bottleneck.
interview: I would also check whether one hot partition is limiting the group. More consumer instances cannot help if there are fewer partitions or uneven keys.
scenario: Consumer lag grows continuously during a traffic spike and remains high even after producers return to normal.
investigation: Check records-per-second produced versus consumed, consumer processing latency, partition count, consumer-group membership, rebalances, downstream database latency and broker health. Measure whether the consumer is CPU-bound, I/O-bound or blocked on a dependency.
prevention: Scale consumers up to the partition limit, batch downstream writes, tune poll and fetch settings carefully, isolate slow dependencies, and use backpressure. Increase partitions only when ordering and key-distribution implications are understood.

title: Kafka consumer reprocesses records after a database commit
short: Kafka commonly gives at-least-once processing semantics. A crash between the business commit and offset commit can produce a duplicate delivery.
answer: I would not try to eliminate every duplicate at the transport layer. I would make the business operation idempotent by storing the event ID with a unique constraint or using a transactional pattern where appropriate. Then replaying the event becomes harmless.
followups: How would you design an inbox table?
mistakes: Do not equate Kafka exactly-once processing with exactly-once effects in an external database.
interview: The interview point is that at-least-once delivery is compatible with exactly-once business outcomes only when the business operation is designed to be idempotent.
scenario: A consumer commits a database transaction and then crashes before the Kafka offset is committed. The same record is delivered again.
investigation: Compare the database transaction boundary with offset commits. Inspect whether processing is idempotent and whether the consumer uses auto-commit or manual acknowledgement.
prevention: Design processing to be idempotent, use an inbox/processed-event table with a unique event ID, or use an appropriate transactional/event-processing pattern when the platform supports it. Never assume at-least-once delivery becomes exactly-once business behavior automatically.

title: Retry policy causes a retry storm across services
short: Retries can improve transient failure recovery, but synchronized or excessive retries can amplify an outage.
answer: I would first quantify retry amplification. Then I would reduce retries at the edge, add exponential backoff with jitter, enforce an overall request deadline and use a circuit breaker. I would also decide which errors are actually retryable rather than retrying every exception.
followups: How do you choose retry counts and deadlines?
mistakes: Never use immediate infinite retries.
interview: The key is to treat retries as load multiplication, not free reliability.
scenario: A downstream inventory service becomes slow. Multiple upstream services retry failed requests, causing traffic to increase dramatically and making the outage worse.
investigation: Look at request rate, retry rate, timeout rate and downstream saturation. Correlate traces to distinguish original requests from retries and calculate the amplification factor.
prevention: Use bounded retries, exponential backoff with jitter, strict deadlines, circuit breakers and retry budgets. Retry only transient and safe operations, and avoid stacking aggressive retries at every service layer.

title: Distributed request latency jumps even though application CPU is normal
short: Normal CPU does not mean the service is healthy. Latency can be caused by blocked threads, exhausted connection pools or a slow dependency.
answer: I would start with a trace rather than guessing from CPU. If most of the three seconds is in a downstream call or waiting for a database connection, I can target the real bottleneck. I would then correlate it with pool saturation and dependency metrics.
followups: What metrics would you put on an API dashboard?
How do you distinguish queueing from downstream latency?
mistakes: Do not use only average latency.
interview: This is why RED metrics and distributed tracing are more useful than CPU alone for request-driven systems.
scenario: p95 latency of an API rises from 250 ms to 3 seconds, but application CPU and memory look normal.
investigation: Use distributed traces to break the request into database, downstream HTTP, cache and queue spans. Compare latency distributions rather than averages and inspect connection pools, thread pools and timeout metrics.
prevention: Instrument all critical boundaries with trace IDs, publish dependency latency/error metrics, and define timeouts and saturation alerts for pools and downstream calls.

title: Outbox publisher sends the same event twice
short: The outbox pattern closes the database-to-message gap, but the publisher can still produce duplicates unless the consumer side is idempotent.
answer: I would keep the outbox because it guarantees the event is durably recorded with the business transaction. Then I would design consumers to deduplicate by event ID. That gives reliable delivery without pretending the publisher can atomically commit an external broker and database.
followups: How do you clean old outbox rows?
mistakes: Do not delete the outbox row before durable publication bookkeeping is complete.
interview: The interview point is that outbox solves atomicity between the local DB change and event intent; it does not magically provide exactly-once external effects.
scenario: A service writes an order and an outbox row in one database transaction. The publisher sends the event, crashes before marking the row as published, and sends it again after restart.
investigation: Inspect outbox status transitions, publisher crash timing and consumer behavior. Verify whether the event has a stable event ID.
prevention: Use a stable event ID and idempotent consumers. Marking the outbox row published is useful for bookkeeping, but it should not be treated as proof that a crash cannot produce a duplicate.

title: Payment succeeds but order service times out
short: An ambiguous timeout must not be treated as failure when an external side effect may already have happened.
answer: I would treat the payment as an uncertain state. I would query or reconcile using a stable idempotency key and provider reference, then update the order asynchronously if needed. The critical rule is never to blindly repeat a charge after an ambiguous timeout.
followups: How would you reconcile payments periodically?
Where does the Saga pattern fit?
mistakes: Do not use only the HTTP response as the source of truth for payment state.
interview: This is a classic distributed-systems problem: you cannot assume the absence of a response means the absence of a side effect.
scenario: The payment provider reports success, but the order service times out before recording the result. A client retry could charge the card again.
investigation: Use the provider transaction/reference ID to query the payment status. Trace whether the request actually reached the provider and whether the callback/webhook was delivered.
prevention: Use an idempotency key at the payment boundary, persist provider references, reconcile uncertain states asynchronously, and model payment as a state machine such as PENDING, SUCCESS, FAILED, UNKNOWN.

title: Database connection pool is exhausted under moderate traffic
short: A connection pool can be exhausted because connections are held too long, not because the database itself is at CPU capacity.
answer: I would check pool acquisition latency and active connection age. Then I would look for slow SQL or transactions that include remote calls. Increasing the pool blindly may move the bottleneck to the database and increase contention.
followups: How do you choose HikariCP pool size?
mistakes: Do not increase pool size without measuring database capacity.
interview: The important distinction is database capacity versus application-side connection occupancy.
scenario: Requests start timing out waiting for database connections, even though database CPU is only 40%.
investigation: Inspect active/idle pool counts, connection acquisition time, slow queries, long transactions and leaked connections. Compare application thread count with pool size.
prevention: Fix slow queries and transaction scope first. Configure sensible pool limits and leak detection, avoid holding connections across remote calls, and monitor acquisition latency.

title: Spring @Async work never runs asynchronously
short: @Async is proxy-based. A direct self-invocation bypasses the proxy and therefore bypasses asynchronous interception.
answer: I would first confirm the executor and proxy path. If the method is called from another method in the same class, I would move the async operation behind another bean or otherwise ensure the invocation crosses the Spring proxy. I would also configure a bounded executor rather than relying on an unbounded default.
followups: How would you propagate MDC or security context?
mistakes: Do not assume an annotation changes execution without proxy interception.
interview: Async is not a magic annotation; proxy interception and executor capacity are both part of the design.
scenario: A method annotated with @Async executes on the caller thread in production.
investigation: Check whether @EnableAsync is configured, whether the method is public, whether the call goes through a Spring proxy, and whether the executor is configured. Look for self-invocation.
prevention: Call the async method through a Spring-managed proxy, configure a bounded executor, propagate required context explicitly, and monitor queue saturation.

title: Spring transaction does not roll back after an exception
short: Spring rollback is based on transaction interception and rollback rules. Catching an exception without marking rollback can allow the transaction to commit.
answer: I would verify the transaction boundary first. If the exception is caught inside the transaction and swallowed, I would either rethrow it or mark the transaction rollback-only. For checked exceptions I would explicitly configure rollback behavior when that matches the business requirement.
mistakes: Do not assume checked exceptions always trigger rollback.
interview: The key is that @Transactional controls a transaction boundary; it does not automatically roll back every exception that ever occurred inside the method.
scenario: A service method annotated with @Transactional catches an exception and returns normally, but the caller expects the database changes to roll back.
investigation: Inspect whether the exception was caught inside the transactional method, whether the exception type matches Spring rollback rules, and whether the call entered through a transaction proxy.
prevention: Let the intended exception propagate or explicitly mark the transaction rollback-only. Configure rollbackFor for checked exceptions when appropriate and avoid self-invocation of transactional methods.

title: Spring application startup becomes much slower after adding a module
short: Slow startup often comes from expensive bean initialization or unnecessary scanning rather than Spring Boot itself.
answer: I would measure startup phases and identify the slow bean or auto-configuration. I would then remove external calls from constructors or initialization paths and reduce unnecessary scanning. I would not optimize startup blindly without a measurement.
followups: How would you troubleshoot a circular dependency?
mistakes: Do not disable broad auto-configurations without understanding what they provide.
interview: Production startup matters for autoscaling and rolling deployments, so startup time is an operational metric.
scenario: Startup time increases from 10 seconds to 45 seconds after a dependency and several configuration classes are added.
investigation: Enable startup metrics or a startup actuator endpoint where appropriate, inspect bean initialization, auto-configuration reports, external calls during bean creation and classpath scanning.
prevention: Avoid network calls during bean construction, reduce unnecessary component scanning, exclude irrelevant auto-configurations when justified, and move expensive work to controlled initialization or asynchronous workflows.

title: SQL query becomes slow after table growth
short: A query can degrade as data volume grows because an old plan or index strategy no longer matches the data distribution.
answer: I would not immediately add an index. I would inspect the execution plan and identify whether the database is scanning too many rows, sorting, or using a poor join strategy. Then I would change the query or index based on evidence and measure again.
followups: When can an index make writes slower?
mistakes: Do not index every column.
interview: The interview answer should emphasize execution plans and selectivity rather than saying indexes always make queries faster.
scenario: A query that used to run in 50 ms now takes 8 seconds after a table grows from one million to fifty million rows.
investigation: Capture the execution plan, inspect row estimates, index usage, selectivity, sort/hash operations and whether predicates are sargable. Compare the plan before and after growth if possible.
prevention: Design indexes based on actual predicates and ordering, rewrite non-sargable expressions, update statistics where applicable, reduce unnecessary columns and consider partitioning only when it solves a demonstrated access pattern.

title: Two services deadlock while updating shared business data
short: Deadlocks happen when transactions hold locks while waiting for each other in a cycle.
answer: I would confirm the cycle in the database deadlock report. The primary fix is to acquire shared resources in a consistent order across code paths. Retries can be a secondary resilience mechanism, but they should not hide a systemic locking problem.
followups: How is a deadlock different from lock timeout?
What isolation level changes might help?
mistakes: Do not rely only on retries.
interview: Consistent lock ordering is often the simplest preventive design.
scenario: Service A updates order then inventory. Service B updates inventory then order. Under concurrency, requests start deadlocking.
investigation: Inspect database deadlock reports and transaction traces to identify lock acquisition order. Confirm whether both operations touch the same rows in opposite order.
prevention: Standardize lock acquisition order, keep transactions short, avoid unnecessary locks, and implement bounded retry for transient deadlock failures.

title: Offset pagination becomes extremely slow on a large table
short: Offset pagination can become expensive at deep pages because the database still processes skipped rows.
answer: For large datasets I would prefer keyset pagination. The client sends the last seen key, and the database can use an index to seek directly into the next range. This gives more stable performance as the page depth increases.
followups: How do you paginate by timestamp safely?
mistakes: Do not claim keyset always works for arbitrary sorting without a stable unique tie-breaker.
interview: The trade-off is that keyset pagination is less convenient for random page-number navigation.
scenario: Page 1 of an API is fast, but requesting page 50,000 takes several seconds.
investigation: Inspect the SQL and execution plan. OFFSET often requires the database to walk past a large number of rows before returning the requested page.
prevention: Use keyset/seek pagination with a stable indexed ordering, such as WHERE id > lastSeenId ORDER BY id LIMIT n. Document that arbitrary page-number jumps may no longer be supported.

title: JWT is valid but a user can access another customer’s resource
short: A valid token proves identity or claims; it does not automatically prove permission to access every resource.
answer: I would explain this as an authorization failure, not a JWT validation failure. The service must verify that the authenticated principal is allowed to access that specific resource, ideally enforcing tenant ownership in the data query as well.
followups: How would you test for this vulnerability?
mistakes: Do not treat possession of a valid JWT as authorization for arbitrary resource IDs.
interview: This is a common IDOR or broken object-level authorization pattern.
scenario: A user with a valid JWT changes an order ID in the URL and receives another customer’s order.
investigation: Inspect authorization at the resource boundary. Verify whether the service checks tenant/user ownership after authentication or only checks that the JWT signature is valid.
prevention: Separate authentication from authorization. Enforce tenant/resource ownership in service and data-access queries, and use defense-in-depth policies where appropriate.

title: Refresh token rotation detects token reuse
short: Refresh-token rotation reduces the window in which a stolen refresh token can be reused undetected.
answer: I would rotate the refresh token on every successful refresh and keep enough server-side state to detect reuse. If an old token is presented after rotation, I would treat that as a possible theft signal and revoke the token family.
followups: How do stateless JWTs get revoked?
Where should refresh tokens be stored?
mistakes: Do not log raw refresh tokens.
interview: Short-lived access tokens limit immediate impact; refresh-token rotation adds detection and containment for longer-lived credentials.
scenario: A refresh token is used twice from different locations. The security team wants the second use to invalidate the session.
investigation: Track refresh-token family state or a server-side token identifier. Detect reuse after rotation and correlate the event with the user/session.
prevention: Rotate refresh tokens on use, store a revocable token family identifier, invalidate the family on reuse, and require re-authentication when compromise is suspected.

title: Kubernetes pods are OOMKilled despite normal application heap usage
short: Container OOMKill can occur when total process memory exceeds the cgroup limit even if Java heap is healthy.
answer: I would compare the container limit with total process memory, not just Xmx. Thread stacks, metaspace and direct buffers can consume significant native memory. Then I would tune the JVM and container together and validate under realistic concurrency.
followups: How do you size Xmx in a container?
mistakes: Do not set Xmx equal to the entire container memory limit.
interview: The distinction between JVM heap and process/container memory is the key interview point.
scenario: A Java pod is repeatedly OOMKilled. JVM heap metrics remain below the configured maximum.
investigation: Compare container memory limits with JVM heap plus native memory, metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers and other process memory. Check cgroup memory events and JVM native-memory diagnostics where available.
prevention: Set container-aware JVM memory settings, leave headroom for native memory, control thread counts and direct buffers, and size the pod limit based on measured total process memory rather than heap alone.

title: Kubernetes readiness probe causes a deployment outage
short: Readiness controls whether a pod receives traffic. A probe that depends on fragile external services can prevent healthy pods from ever entering service.
answer: I would make the readiness endpoint reflect whether the application itself can accept traffic, not whether every dependency is perfect. Downstream failures should normally be handled at request time through resilience patterns.
followups: When should startup probes be used?
mistakes: Do not make liveness depend on downstream services.
interview: Overly strict health checks can turn a dependency outage into a deployment-wide outage.
scenario: New pods start, but the readiness probe immediately fails because the application depends on a downstream service that is temporarily unavailable.
investigation: Check probe endpoint behavior and whether readiness is being used to represent application availability versus dependency readiness. Inspect startup and dependency initialization logs.
prevention: Keep readiness lightweight and local. Let the service become ready when it can serve valid requests, while handling downstream dependency failures with timeouts and resilience rather than making the readiness probe depend on every dependency.

title: Order database migration must happen without downtime
short: Zero-downtime schema changes require compatibility between database and application versions during rollout.
answer: I would avoid a destructive migration in the same deployment as the application change. I would expand the schema first, deploy backward-compatible code, backfill gradually, switch traffic, and contract later after old versions are gone.
followups: How do you backfill 500 million rows safely?
What metrics would you monitor during the migration?
mistakes: Do not assume DDL is always instant or lock-free.
interview: The key is to design migrations around the overlap period during rolling deployment.
scenario: A column must change in a high-traffic orders table while old and new application versions run simultaneously during a rolling deployment.
investigation: Identify whether the change is backward-compatible. Check write/read behavior of old and new versions and estimate lock duration and table rewrite cost.
prevention: Use expand-and-contract: add the new structure first, deploy code that can read/write both forms if needed, backfill in batches, switch reads, then remove the old structure in a later deployment.

title: Notification provider becomes unavailable during a traffic burst
short: A notification system should absorb provider outages instead of making every user request wait for the provider.
answer: I would decouple user-facing operations from notification delivery with a durable queue. Workers can retry with backoff and provider-specific limits, while a circuit breaker prevents an unhealthy provider from consuming all worker capacity.
followups: How do you guarantee no duplicate notifications?
How would you prioritize urgent notifications?
mistakes: Do not let retries grow without a queue or budget.
interview: This is primarily an asynchronous workload and should be designed around durability, backpressure and eventual delivery.
scenario: Email/SMS provider latency spikes and then returns errors while the platform is processing millions of notifications.
investigation: Measure provider error rate and latency, queue depth, retry rate and message age. Check whether the application is making synchronous provider calls or buffering work.
prevention: Queue notification requests, apply provider-specific rate limits, retry transient failures with backoff, route to a secondary provider where justified, and preserve message state for reconciliation.

title: Spring REST endpoint returns 500 because validation exceptions bypass the global handler
short: Validation failures should normally be translated into a consistent client-facing 4xx response rather than leaking as 500 errors.
answer: I would inspect the actual exception type first. Then I would add a targeted global handler for validation and binding failures and return a stable error format with field-level messages. I would add integration tests so every controller follows the same contract.
followups: How do you validate path variables?
How do you avoid exposing internal exception messages?
mistakes: Do not return stack traces to clients.
interview: Do not assume every validation failure arrives as MethodArgumentNotValidException; the exact exception depends on how validation is triggered.
scenario: Invalid request payloads sometimes produce inconsistent 400/500 responses depending on the controller.
investigation: Inspect exception types thrown by request binding/validation and compare them with the @ControllerAdvice handlers. Verify whether handler methods cover the actual framework exception types.
prevention: Define a consistent error contract, handle validation/binding exceptions centrally, and test malformed payloads across controllers.

title: Spring cache serves stale data after an update
short: Caching introduces a second copy of data, so the application must define how and when that copy becomes stale.
answer: I would first verify whether the write invalidates the exact cache key after the database transaction succeeds. In a multi-instance system I would prefer a shared cache or an invalidation mechanism rather than assuming local caches are consistent.
followups: How do you prevent cache stampede?
What happens if the cache is unavailable?
mistakes: Do not invalidate the cache before a failed database write unless the policy is deliberate.
interview: Cache consistency is a business trade-off. The interview answer should state the acceptable staleness requirement.
scenario: An update succeeds in the database, but subsequent GET requests still return the old value from the cache.
investigation: Check cache eviction/update semantics, transaction timing, cache key consistency and whether multiple application instances maintain independent local caches.
prevention: Use a clear cache-aside policy, evict or update the cache after a successful write, and use a shared cache when cross-instance consistency is required. Define an acceptable staleness window.

title: A SQL query causes lock contention during a batch job
short: Long-running batch transactions can create lock contention even when the individual SQL statements are fast.
answer: I would reduce transaction scope and batch size first, then inspect lock waits and the access plan. The batch should acquire locks predictably and release them frequently enough that interactive traffic can make progress.
followups: How would you throttle a backfill?
mistakes: Do not solve lock contention only by increasing database resources.
interview: The best batch size is workload-specific; measure lock duration and throughput rather than picking a huge fixed number.
scenario: A nightly batch update causes daytime API requests to wait on locked rows.
investigation: Inspect transaction duration, lock wait events, batch size and whether the batch scans or updates rows in a conflicting order.
prevention: Break work into smaller committed batches, process in deterministic key order, use appropriate indexes, schedule heavy work carefully and avoid holding locks while doing unrelated work.

title: A service leaks ThreadLocal state between requests
short: ThreadLocal values belong to the worker thread, not the request. In pooled executors, the same thread can process many requests.
answer: I would treat ThreadLocal as thread-scoped state and ensure every set has a corresponding remove in a finally block. For request context, I would prefer framework-managed mechanisms when possible. I would also test thread reuse explicitly.
followups: Why can it cause memory leaks?
mistakes: Do not assume a pooled thread is dedicated to one request.
interview: The bug can become both a data-isolation problem and a memory-retention problem.
scenario: A long-running servlet application shows request/user context from one request appearing in a later request handled by the same worker thread.
investigation: Inspect ThreadLocal usage and thread-pool lifecycle. Check whether values are removed in finally blocks and whether pooled threads are reused across requests.
prevention: Set request-scoped context at the boundary and always remove ThreadLocal values in finally. Prefer framework-managed request context where available.

title: CompletableFuture chain silently loses exceptions
short: CompletableFuture failures are stored in the future. They do not automatically become visible to the caller unless the chain is observed or joined.
answer: I would ensure the controller or service returns the composed future or explicitly waits at the correct boundary. Then I would handle failures with exceptionally or handle and log the original cause with correlation context.
followups: How do you add a timeout to a future?
mistakes: Do not ignore a future returned by an important operation.
interview: The interview trap is assuming asynchronous exceptions behave exactly like synchronous exceptions.
scenario: An asynchronous workflow returns a successful HTTP response even though one of the CompletableFuture stages failed.
investigation: Trace the future chain and inspect whether exceptionally/handle/whenComplete or join/get is used. Check whether a failed stage is created but its result is ignored.
prevention: Compose the futures into one returned future, handle exceptions explicitly at the boundary, and avoid launching independent futures whose failures are never observed.

title: JVM GC pauses increase after a traffic increase
short: GC latency is influenced by allocation rate, live-set size and collector behavior, not simply by total heap size.
answer: I would first correlate GC pauses with latency and inspect allocation and promotion rates. Then I would determine whether the issue is excessive allocation, an unexpectedly large live set or collector configuration. I would change one variable at a time and validate with realistic load.
followups: How does G1 work at a high level?
What is a memory leak in Java?
mistakes: Do not equate high heap usage with a GC bug automatically.
interview: Never start by increasing the heap without understanding why the live set or allocation rate changed.
scenario: p99 latency increases because occasional GC pauses grow from tens of milliseconds to over a second after traffic increases.
investigation: Inspect allocation rate, heap occupancy, GC pause times, old-generation promotion and object-retention patterns. Correlate GC events with request latency.
prevention: Reduce unnecessary allocations, investigate retained objects, choose/tune the collector based on measured behavior, size the heap appropriately and validate changes with production-like load.

title: What is the happens-before relationship in Java?
short: Happens-before defines an ordering that guarantees visibility of one action to another thread.
answer: It is established by synchronization actions such as unlocking then locking the same monitor, volatile writes/read pairs, thread start/join and other concurrency constructs. It is stronger than simply saying one line executed earlier in wall-clock time.
followups: Can instruction reordering break an unsynchronized program?
interview: Happens-before is the JMM visibility and ordering guarantee. I look for an established synchronization edge rather than assuming timing makes a write visible.
scenario: Happens-before defines an ordering that guarantees visibility of one action to another thread.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: Why is double-checked locking safe only with volatile?
short: The singleton reference must be volatile so publication and initialization writes are correctly ordered.
answer: Without volatile, a thread can observe a non-null reference before all constructor writes are visible because publication and initialization can be reordered. Volatile prevents that unsafe publication pattern.
followups: Why is the first null check needed?
Can an enum singleton avoid this complexity?
interview: Double-checked locking needs a volatile instance reference. The volatile write publishes the fully initialized object with the required visibility and ordering guarantees.

title: What is CAS and how is it used in Java concurrency?
short: Compare-and-set atomically changes a value only if it still equals an expected value.
answer: AtomicInteger and many concurrent structures use CAS loops. CAS avoids blocking for some operations, but high contention can cause repeated retries and does not automatically solve multi-variable invariants.
interview: CAS is an optimistic atomic primitive: compare the current value with the expected value and update only when they match. Java atomics build lock-free algorithms from it.

title: What is a lock-free algorithm?
short: A lock-free algorithm guarantees that system-wide progress continues even if individual threads are delayed.
answer: It commonly uses atomic operations such as CAS. Lock-free does not mean wait-free: one thread can still starve while others make progress.
interview: Lock-free means some thread can always make progress. I would use it only when the workload justifies the complexity and after measuring contention.

title: What is the ABA problem?
short: ABA occurs when a value changes from A to B and back to A, making a CAS unable to detect that an intermediate change happened.
answer: Algorithms can use stamped or versioned references to distinguish logically different states that have the same raw value. It matters in non-blocking algorithms and reused nodes.
followups: Can ABA matter in ordinary HashMap code?
interview: The ABA problem is a false assumption that A is unchanged because the current value is A. Version stamps can make the state transition detectable.

title: How does String.intern() work?
short: intern returns a canonical pooled representation of a string.
answer: The JVM maintains a string pool. Interning can reduce duplicate string storage when there are many repeated values, but excessive interning can increase pool pressure and should not be used as a generic performance trick.
followups: Is the string pool on the heap?
interview: intern gives equal strings a shared canonical instance. I use it only when profiling and data characteristics justify it.

title: What is escape analysis in the JVM?
short: Escape analysis lets the JVM determine whether an object or lock escapes a method or thread.
answer: The JIT can use that information for optimizations such as scalar replacement and lock elimination in suitable cases. It is an optimization, so application code should not depend on a specific optimization occurring.
followups: Can all short-lived objects be stack allocated?
interview: Escape analysis can let the JIT eliminate allocations or synchronization when it proves they are unnecessary. I treat it as a runtime optimization and verify with profiling.

title: How does JIT compilation improve Java performance?
short: The JIT compiles frequently executed bytecode into optimized native machine code at runtime.
answer: It uses runtime profiling to optimize hot paths, inline calls, eliminate checks and apply speculative optimizations. Deoptimization can occur when assumptions stop being valid.
interview: Java starts with bytecode execution and the JIT optimizes hot code using runtime information. Warm-up and workload shape therefore matter in benchmarks.

title: What is class initialization order in Java?
short: Class initialization runs static initialization when the class is first actively used.
answer: Superclass initialization precedes subclass initialization, and static fields/blocks execute in textual order within a class. Initialization is synchronized by the JVM so the class is initialized once.
interview: I remember the order as parent class initialization first, then the subclass, with static fields and blocks following source order.

title: How can ClassLoader leaks happen in application servers?
short: A class loader can remain reachable through threads, ThreadLocals, static references or registered callbacks after an application is undeployed.
answer: If the loader cannot be garbage collected, all classes and metadata it loaded may remain reachable, causing metaspace growth across redeployments.
followups: How do you diagnose a classloader leak?
interview: In containers I look for long-lived threads, ThreadLocals, static caches and libraries that retain the application ClassLoader. Cleanup at shutdown is essential.

title: What is the difference between heap and metaspace?
short: Heap stores ordinary Java objects, while metaspace stores class metadata outside the traditional Java heap.
answer: Heap pressure usually manifests as GC and heap OOMs. Metaspace pressure can grow when many classes or class loaders are created, especially in plugin or redeployment scenarios.
interview: Heap and metaspace are different memory areas with different failure symptoms. I check the correct metric before tuning -Xmx or metaspace settings.

title: How do records affect equality and immutability?
short: Records provide concise data carriers with generated accessors, equals, hashCode and toString based on components.
answer: A record is shallowly immutable: its component references are final, but referenced mutable objects can still change. Records are excellent for value-like DTOs and keys.
interview: Records reduce boilerplate for value objects. I still consider defensive copies when a component is a mutable collection or array.

title: What are sealed classes useful for?
short: Sealed classes restrict which classes can extend or implement a type.
answer: They make a closed hierarchy explicit and can improve modeling and exhaustiveness in pattern matching. The permitted subclasses must follow the sealing rules.
followups: Can a sealed class have an indirect subclass?
interview: Sealed classes are useful when a domain has a deliberately closed set of variants, such as payment states or command results.

title: What is pattern matching for instanceof?
short: Pattern matching lets an instanceof test declare and bind the matching variable.
answer: It reduces repetitive casts and makes conditional logic clearer. The variable's scope follows the compiler's flow analysis.
interview: It combines the type check and cast, improving readability without changing the underlying object model.

title: What is structured concurrency conceptually?
short: Structured concurrency treats related concurrent tasks as one scoped unit of work.
answer: The parent task controls the lifetime of child tasks, making cancellation, failure propagation and resource management easier to reason about. In Java it is associated with newer concurrency APIs and remains a design concept worth understanding.
followups: How is it different from CompletableFuture?
interview: Structured concurrency makes concurrent subtasks have a clear parent scope, so failures and cancellation can be handled together instead of leaving orphaned work.

title: How does interruption work in Java?
short: Interruption is a cooperative cancellation signal delivered to a thread.
answer: Blocking methods may throw InterruptedException, while code should either propagate it or restore the interrupt flag after handling it. Swallowing interruption can break shutdown and cancellation behavior.
followups: Is interrupt the same as stopping a thread?
interview: I treat interruption as a cancellation request. If I catch InterruptedException and cannot propagate it, I restore the interrupt flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt().

title: How do you benchmark Java code correctly?
short: Microbenchmarks must account for warm-up, JIT optimization, dead-code elimination and measurement noise.
answer: JMH handles forks, warm-up iterations and measurement infrastructure. For production decisions, microbenchmarks should complement end-to-end profiling rather than replace it.
interview: I use JMH for small JVM benchmarks and real workload tests for service behavior. I never trust a single System.nanoTime loop as a performance conclusion.

title: What is the difference between fail-fast and fail-safe iteration?
short: Fail-fast iterators may detect structural modification and throw ConcurrentModificationException, while snapshot or concurrent collections use different semantics.
answer: Fail-fast is a best-effort bug detector, not a thread-safety guarantee. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates over a snapshot, while concurrent collections provide their own weakly consistent semantics.
interview: Concurrent iteration semantics depend on the collection. I never use fail-fast behavior as synchronization.

title: How does Spring resolve bean dependencies?
short: Spring resolves required beans from the ApplicationContext using type, qualifiers, primary candidates and other metadata.
answer: Dependency resolution considers type and qualifiers and can fail on ambiguity or missing beans. Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit and supports immutable components.
followups: What happens with two beans of the same type?
interview: I prefer constructor injection because dependencies are explicit and the object cannot be created without them. Qualifier or primary resolves intentional ambiguity.

title: Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?
short: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit and supports immutability and easier testing.
answer: The object can be instantiated with all required collaborators, fields can be final, and missing dependencies fail early. Field injection hides dependencies and complicates plain unit tests.
interview: For required dependencies I use constructors. It improves design and makes the class valid immediately after construction.

title: How does Spring handle circular dependencies?
short: A circular dependency occurs when bean A requires B while B requires A.
answer: Some setter/field injection cases can be resolved through early references, but constructor cycles cannot be satisfied normally. The best fix is usually redesigning responsibilities rather than relying on lazy workarounds.
interview: I treat circular dependencies as a design smell. I first split responsibilities or introduce a domain service rather than hiding the cycle with @Lazy.

title: What is BeanPostProcessor?
short: BeanPostProcessor hooks into bean creation before and after initialization.
answer: Spring uses post-processors for concerns such as dependency injection, annotation processing and proxy creation. This is a major extension point in the container lifecycle.
interview: BeanPostProcessor lets Spring inspect or wrap beans during creation. Many framework features are implemented through these lifecycle extension points.
scenario: BeanPostProcessor hooks into bean creation before and after initialization.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is BeanFactoryPostProcessor?
short: It can modify bean definitions before regular beans are instantiated.
answer: It operates on metadata rather than bean instances. This distinction is important when understanding configuration processing and how Spring prepares the container.
interview: BeanFactoryPostProcessor changes bean definitions before bean instantiation; BeanPostProcessor works with bean instances during lifecycle processing.

title: How does @Lazy affect Spring bean creation?
short: @Lazy defers bean creation until it is first needed.
answer: It can reduce startup cost but moves initialization latency to first use and can hide configuration errors until runtime. It should not be used to paper over dependency design problems.
followups: When is it a bad idea?
interview: Lazy initialization can improve startup, but it trades startup work for first-use latency and delayed failures.

title: How does Spring's transaction interceptor decide commit or rollback?
short: The transaction interceptor starts or joins a transaction, invokes the target, then commits or rolls back based on outcome and rollback rules.
answer: By default, runtime exceptions and errors trigger rollback in typical declarative transaction handling, while checked exceptions may require explicit rollback configuration. The actual behavior depends on the transaction manager and rules.
followups: How do you roll back for checked exceptions?
What if an exception is caught inside the method?
interview: I explain that the proxy surrounds the method, begins or joins a transaction, and commits on successful completion or rolls back according to configured rollback rules.

title: What is read-only transaction optimization?
short: readOnly is a transaction hint indicating that the transaction is intended for reads.
answer: It can influence ORM flush behavior or database handling depending on the stack, but it is not a universal enforcement that prevents writes. It should not replace authorization or application-level rules.
interview: readOnly communicates intent and may reduce unnecessary flush work, but I don't treat it as a hard write prohibition.

title: How does Spring Retry differ from manual retries?
short: Spring Retry centralizes retry policy through annotations or interceptors.
answer: It can manage attempts, backoff and exception classification, but retrying still requires idempotency and timeout boundaries. A framework does not make unsafe operations safe to repeat.
interview: Retry policy should be explicit and bounded. Whether implemented with Spring Retry or manually, I need idempotency, backoff and a clear list of retryable failures.

title: How do you test a transactional service correctly?
short: Transactional tests should verify both database state and transaction boundaries.
answer: Use integration tests when behavior depends on real transaction semantics, rollback, isolation or JPA flush behavior. Unit tests can cover business branching without requiring a database.
interview: I use unit tests for business logic and integration tests for actual transaction behavior, especially rollback and persistence-context semantics.

title: What is Testcontainers useful for?
short: Testcontainers runs real infrastructure such as databases or brokers in disposable containers for tests.
answer: It improves fidelity compared with mocks or embedded substitutes and is valuable for SQL dialect, migrations and integration behavior.
followups: How do you keep tests fast?
interview: For persistence or messaging integration tests, Testcontainers gives me the real dependency and catches environment-specific behavior earlier.

title: How do you avoid leaking sensitive actuator information?
short: Operational endpoints can expose environment, mappings or metrics that may reveal sensitive details.
answer: Expose only required endpoints, secure them with authentication/authorization, and avoid returning secrets in configuration or error payloads. Network restrictions can provide another layer.
interview: Actuator should be treated as an operational API. I expose the minimum surface and secure sensitive endpoints separately from public application endpoints.

title: How should correlation IDs be propagated in Spring services?
short: A correlation ID links logs and traces belonging to the same request flow.
answer: Generate one at the edge if absent, validate/limit incoming values, put it into request context and propagate it to downstream calls and logs. Distributed tracing can provide richer context.
followups: How do you propagate across async execution?
interview: I establish correlation at the ingress boundary and propagate it consistently. I also ensure it cannot be used to inject arbitrary log control characters or sensitive data.

title: What is Spring's application event mechanism good for?
short: Application events decouple in-process publishers from listeners.
answer: They are useful for local domain notifications, but they are not a durable distributed message broker. If a business event must survive process failure, use durable messaging or an outbox.
followups: How do you make listeners async?
interview: Spring events are in-process. I use them for local decoupling, not as a replacement for Kafka when durability and cross-service delivery matter.

title: How does @TransactionalEventListener work?
short: It can execute a listener at a transaction phase such as after commit.
answer: This is useful when an in-process action should occur only after successful commit. It is still local to the application and can be lost if the process dies before the listener executes.
interview: For post-commit local work I can use @TransactionalEventListener, but for durable external events I prefer an outbox because application events are not a durable queue.

title: How do you handle large file uploads in Spring Boot?
short: Large uploads should avoid buffering entire files in application memory.
answer: Use streaming or multipart handling with size limits, content validation, temporary storage and preferably object storage for large payloads. Scan or validate files before making them available.
followups: How do you prevent disk exhaustion?
How do you secure uploaded files?
interview: I enforce request-size limits, stream large content, validate type and size, and use object storage rather than keeping large files in JVM memory.

title: How should pagination be implemented in a REST API?
short: Pagination limits response size and controls database work.
answer: For large mutable datasets, stable ordering plus keyset pagination is often safer than deep offsets. The API should define limits and deterministic ordering.
followups: How do you handle deleted rows?
interview: I cap page size and use deterministic ordering. For large sequential datasets I prefer keyset pagination to avoid deep OFFSET costs.

title: How do you design API idempotency in Spring Boot?
short: Idempotency keys let clients safely retry operations without creating duplicate business effects.
answer: Store a key scoped to the client and operation with a unique constraint and outcome. Handle concurrent duplicate requests atomically.
followups: What if two requests arrive simultaneously?
interview: I implement idempotency at the service boundary with a durable key and unique constraint, then return the original result for safe retries.

title: How do you handle timeouts in WebClient?
short: HTTP client calls need bounded connection, response and overall operation timeouts.
answer: A timeout should align with the end-to-end deadline and be observable. Retrying after a timeout is only safe when the operation is idempotent or otherwise protected.
followups: How do you prevent hanging connections?
interview: I set bounded timeouts at the client and propagate the request deadline. I don't treat timeout as automatically retryable because the downstream may have already processed the request.

title: How do you make scheduled Spring jobs safe in multiple instances?
short: A scheduled method runs in every application instance unless coordinated.
answer: For cluster-wide singleton work, use a distributed lock, leader election or move the job to a dedicated scheduler/queue. The job itself should also be idempotent.
followups: What if the lock holder crashes?
interview: In a horizontally scaled service I never assume @Scheduled runs once globally. I use a distributed coordination mechanism or a dedicated job runner.
scenario: A scheduled method runs in every application instance unless coordinated.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is the difference between orchestration and choreography in Saga?
short: Orchestration uses a coordinator to direct steps; choreography lets services react to events without a central coordinator.
answer: Orchestration makes workflow visibility and compensation ordering explicit, while choreography reduces central coupling but can become difficult to trace as the number of participants grows.
interview: I choose orchestration when the workflow is complex and needs centralized visibility; choreography can work well for simpler event-driven flows.
scenario: Orchestration uses a coordinator to direct steps; choreography lets services react to events without a central coordinator.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: How do you make a Saga compensation idempotent?
short: A compensation may be retried, so it must safely produce the same final state when applied more than once.
answer: Use a unique operation ID, state checks and conditional updates. Compensation should be a business action rather than assuming the exact inverse of every original operation exists.
interview: I give each Saga step and compensation a stable operation ID and make the state transition conditional and repeatable.
scenario: A compensation may be retried, so it must safely produce the same final state when applied more than once.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is a distributed lock and what are its risks?
short: A distributed lock coordinates access to a resource across multiple service instances.
answer: Risks include lease expiry, clock assumptions, client pauses and split-brain behavior. Use fencing tokens or database constraints where correctness is critical rather than relying solely on a lock.
followups: Why can a lock expire while work continues?
interview: A distributed lock is not magic mutual exclusion. For critical correctness I combine leases with fencing or durable database constraints.
scenario: A distributed lock coordinates access to a resource across multiple service instances.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is a fencing token?
short: A fencing token is a monotonically increasing value that lets a resource reject stale lock holders.
answer: When a new lock owner gets a higher token, the storage layer accepts only operations carrying the current or newer token. This protects against a paused old owner resuming later.
interview: Fencing converts a time-based lock into a verifiable ordering at the resource, preventing stale owners from corrupting state.
scenario: A fencing token is a monotonically increasing value that lets a resource reject stale lock holders.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: How do you handle clock skew in distributed systems?
short: Different machines can have clocks that differ, so wall-clock timestamps are not safe for every ordering decision.
answer: Use logical clocks, sequence numbers, database ordering or server-side timestamps when strict ordering matters. Keep NTP synchronized but don't assume perfect clocks.
followups: How does clock skew affect JWT expiry?
interview: I use monotonic sequence numbers or authoritative storage for ordering. Wall-clock time is useful for observability but not always for correctness.
scenario: Different machines can have clocks that differ, so wall-clock timestamps are not safe for every ordering decision.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is backpressure and where should it be applied?
short: Backpressure limits producers when consumers cannot keep up.
answer: It can be implemented with bounded queues, concurrency limits, broker flow control and admission control. Without it, queues grow until latency or memory becomes unacceptable.
followups: What should happen when capacity is exhausted?
interview: Backpressure is a capacity-protection mechanism. I prefer bounded queues and explicit overload behavior over unlimited buffering.
scenario: Backpressure limits producers when consumers cannot keep up.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is hedged request processing?
short: Hedging sends a duplicate request after a delay to reduce tail latency.
answer: It can improve p99 when latency variance is high, but it increases load and can duplicate side effects. It is best suited to idempotent reads with capacity headroom.
followups: How do you choose the hedge delay?
interview: Hedging is a latency optimization that spends extra capacity. I use it only for safe idempotent operations and after measuring tail latency.
scenario: Hedging sends a duplicate request after a delay to reduce tail latency.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: How do you prevent a thundering herd during cache recovery?
short: Many clients may simultaneously miss a cache after restart or mass expiry.
answer: Use request coalescing, staggered warming, TTL jitter and bounded database concurrency. A single lock around every key can become another bottleneck.
followups: How do you warm a cache safely?
interview: I protect the backing store with coalescing and bounded concurrency, then warm hot keys gradually rather than letting every request rebuild them.
scenario: Many clients may simultaneously miss a cache after restart or mass expiry.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is a dead-letter queue versus a retry topic?
short: A retry topic delays another processing attempt, while a dead-letter destination holds messages that exceeded the retry policy or are otherwise non-processable.
answer: Retry destinations are part of normal transient-failure handling. DLTs are an operational quarantine and should include metadata for diagnosis and replay.
interview: I use retry topics for transient failures and a DLT for exhausted or invalid messages. Both need observability and a safe replay path.

title: How do Kafka transactions help exactly-once processing?
short: Kafka transactions can atomically publish records and commit consumer offsets for Kafka-to-Kafka processing.
answer: Exactly-once semantics are bounded by the Kafka processing model; external side effects such as a database update still need idempotency or transactional integration.
interview: Kafka transactions can provide strong semantics within Kafka, but they do not magically make a database and Kafka one atomic transaction. External effects still need a design.
scenario: Kafka transactions can atomically publish records and commit consumer offsets for Kafka-to-Kafka processing.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: How do you design Kafka partition keys?
short: The partition key determines which partition receives a record and therefore where per-key ordering is preserved.
answer: Choose a key that matches the business ordering requirement and distributes load. A hot key can overload one partition even when the topic has many partitions.
followups: Can you change the key later?
interview: I choose the key based on ordering first, then validate distribution. If one entity is extremely hot, I may need a different model because ordering and parallelism conflict.
scenario: The partition key determines which partition receives a record and therefore where per-key ordering is preserved.

prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is consumer group parallelism in Kafka?
short: Within a consumer group, a partition is processed by one consumer at a time.
answer: Adding consumers increases parallelism only until all partitions are assigned. More partitions can increase throughput but also affect ordering, storage and operational cost.
followups: Can two consumers read the same partition?
interview: Consumer count cannot exceed useful partition parallelism. I size partitions for expected throughput and future concurrency, not just current traffic.

title: How do you design a reliable webhook delivery system?
short: Webhook delivery should assume receivers are slow, unavailable and duplicate-prone.
answer: Persist delivery attempts, sign payloads, use bounded retries with backoff, timeouts, idempotency guidance and a dead-letter state. Track delivery status for operators.
followups: How do you avoid retry storms?
interview: I persist the event and delivery state, sign requests, retry transient failures with backoff, and make the receiver contract idempotent because duplicate delivery is expected.
scenario: Webhook delivery should assume receivers are slow, unavailable and duplicate-prone.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: How do you version a microservice event without breaking consumers?
short: Event compatibility requires planned evolution rather than ad-hoc field changes.
answer: Prefer additive changes and tolerant readers. For breaking semantics, use an explicit version or new event type and migrate consumers gradually.
interview: I treat events as contracts. Additive changes are preferred; semantic or structural breaks get explicit versioning and a migration window.

title: What is service mesh and when would you use it?
short: A service mesh moves common service-to-service networking concerns into infrastructure sidecars or nodes.
answer: It can provide mTLS, traffic policy, retries, telemetry and routing without duplicating logic in every service, but adds operational complexity and another failure surface.
interview: A service mesh can standardize cross-service networking, but I adopt it only when the organization can operate the added control plane and data-plane complexity.
scenario: A service mesh moves common service-to-service networking concerns into infrastructure sidecars or nodes.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: How do you design a circuit breaker around a flaky dependency?
short: A circuit breaker prevents repeated calls to an unhealthy dependency.
answer: It transitions among closed, open and half-open states based on failures or slow calls. Thresholds should reflect business impact and avoid treating every transient error as permanent.
interview: I use a bounded timeout first, then circuit breaking to stop repeated load when failure rates or latency cross thresholds. Recovery probes happen gradually.

title: How do you distinguish an application retry from a broker redelivery?
short: Application retry is an explicit second attempt, while broker redelivery happens when offsets are not committed or delivery semantics cause a record to be seen again.
answer: Observability should record attempt count and event ID. Treat both as expected duplicate paths and keep processing idempotent.
interview: I distinguish transport-level redelivery from business-level retries in telemetry. Both can create duplicates, so the consumer must remain idempotent.
scenario: Application retry is an explicit second attempt, while broker redelivery happens when offsets are not committed or delivery semantics cause a record to be seen again.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: How do you handle a downstream dependency that returns slow 200 responses?
short: A successful but slow dependency can exhaust threads and connections just like errors.
answer: Use deadlines, connection limits, concurrency bulkheads, circuit breakers based on slow-call rate, and fallbacks where safe. Monitor p95/p99 rather than only error rate.
followups: What is a slow-call circuit breaker?
How do you protect the thread pool?
interview: Latency is a failure mode. I configure slow-call thresholds and capacity controls, not just error retries, because slow success can still take down callers.
scenario: A successful but slow dependency can exhaust threads and connections just like errors.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is the difference between at-most-once, at-least-once and effectively-once processing?
short: These describe how many times processing may occur from the application's perspective.
answer: At-most-once may lose messages but avoids duplicates; at-least-once may duplicate; effectively-once combines at-least-once transport with idempotent business processing so the observable effect occurs once.
followups: How do you make a consumer idempotent?
interview: I prefer at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers for many backend systems. Exactly-once transport alone does not solve external side effects.
scenario: These describe how many times processing may occur from the application's perspective.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is a partial index and when is it useful?
short: A partial or filtered index indexes only rows satisfying a predicate.
answer: It can reduce index size and improve targeted queries when a stable subset is frequently accessed, such as active records. Support and syntax vary by database.
followups: What happens when the predicate changes?
interview: A partial index is useful when a query repeatedly targets a subset of rows. I verify that the optimizer can use it and that the predicate matches the workload.

title: What is an index-only scan?
short: An index-only scan can satisfy a query using index data without visiting the base table when visibility and required columns permit.
answer: It can reduce I/O, especially for covering indexes, but maintenance cost and visibility rules still matter.
followups: How is it different from a covering index?
interview: Index-only access can be very fast for read-heavy queries, but I balance wider indexes against write and storage overhead.

title: How do foreign keys affect performance?
short: Foreign keys enforce referential integrity but can add work to inserts, updates and deletes.
answer: Referenced and referencing columns should be indexed appropriately for common operations. Constraints are usually worth the correctness they provide, but large cascades need careful design.
interview: Foreign keys protect correctness. I index the referencing columns when needed and pay attention to cascade behavior on large tables.

title: What is a database connection leak?
short: A connection leak occurs when application code fails to return a borrowed connection to the pool.
answer: Over time active connections reach the pool maximum and requests wait or fail. Proper resource management, pool leak detection and metrics help diagnose it.
followups: Why does traffic make the issue worse?
interview: I correlate pool active count and pending acquisition with code paths. In JDBC, try-with-resources and framework-managed transactions prevent many leaks.

title: What is MVCC?
short: Multi-version concurrency control lets readers and writers operate using versions of rows rather than blocking each other in the simplest cases.
answer: Different databases implement MVCC differently. It improves read/write concurrency but creates version cleanup and isolation considerations.
interview: MVCC maintains multiple row versions so readers can see a consistent snapshot while writers proceed. Exact semantics depend on the database.

title: How do database locks escalate?
short: Some database systems can replace many fine-grained locks with a coarser lock to reduce lock-management overhead.
answer: Escalation can increase contention and cause unexpected blocking during large operations. Batching and appropriate indexes can reduce the number of locked rows.
interview: Lock escalation is a database-specific behavior where many locks can become a larger lock. Large batch operations should be designed with this possibility in mind.
scenario: Some database systems can replace many fine-grained locks with a coarser lock to reduce lock-management overhead.
