prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is parameterized SQL and why does it matter?
short: Parameterized SQL separates SQL structure from user-supplied values.
answer: Prepared statements prevent input from being interpreted as SQL syntax and can also improve plan reuse depending on the database.
interview: I always bind user values through prepared statements or framework parameters. String concatenation is both unsafe and harder to maintain.

title: How do you implement an idempotent database command?
short: An idempotent command produces the same final state when safely repeated.
answer: Use unique business keys, upserts, compare-and-set updates or state checks. The database constraint should enforce uniqueness where correctness depends on it.
followups: How do you handle duplicate requests?
interview: I prefer database-enforced uniqueness and conditional state transitions over relying only on application checks.

title: What is a covering query and why can SELECT * be harmful?
short: A query is easier to cover when it selects only the columns it needs.
answer: SELECT * increases network payload, deserialization and the set of columns an index must cover. Schema changes can also unexpectedly change its cost.
followups: Why is it a maintenance risk?
interview: I select only required columns, especially in APIs and hot queries. It keeps payloads smaller and gives indexes a realistic chance to cover the access path.

title: How do you find gaps in sequential IDs?
short: Gaps can be identified by comparing each value with the previous value or expected sequence.
answer: Window functions such as LAG can reveal discontinuities. Whether gaps are a problem depends on the ID generation strategy; auto-increment sequences commonly allow gaps.
followups: Why are auto-increment IDs not gapless?
When do you need a business sequence?
interview: I can detect gaps with LAG or generate an expected sequence, but I don't assume IDs must be gapless because transaction rollback and sequence caching can create gaps.

title: What is a recursive CTE useful for?
short: A recursive CTE queries hierarchical or graph-like relationships such as employee-manager trees.
answer: It has an anchor query and a recursive member and needs termination conditions. Large or cyclic graphs require safeguards.
followups: When would you use application traversal?
interview: Recursive CTEs are useful for hierarchies when the database supports them. I define a clear termination condition and protect against cycles or excessive depth.

title: How do you detect skew in a database workload?
short: Skew means a small subset of keys or queries receives disproportionate traffic or data.
answer: Hot tenants, hot rows and popular products can create contention even when average load looks healthy. Partitioning, caching and sharding strategies must account for skew.
followups: How do hot rows cause contention?
How do you mitigate hot keys?
interview: I look at per-key and per-query distributions, not just averages. A hot key can dominate latency and CPU even when overall utilization seems moderate.
scenario: Skew means a small subset of keys or queries receives disproportionate traffic or data.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is write amplification in databases?
short: Write amplification means the system performs more physical or logical writes than the application-level change suggests.
answer: Indexes, WAL/redo logs, page splits, replication and secondary structures can all add write work. It affects storage, I/O and throughput.
interview: Adding indexes improves reads but increases write amplification because every insert/update may maintain more structures.

title: How do you safely change a primary key type on a large table?
short: Changing a key type on a large table can require coordinated changes to indexes, foreign keys and application code.
answer: Use an expand-and-contract migration: introduce the new key representation, backfill, support both versions, migrate references, validate, then remove the old structure.
followups: How do you backfill without blocking?
interview: I avoid an in-place destructive change. I introduce the new representation compatibly, migrate references incrementally and remove the old key only after all consumers are moved.

title: How do you investigate lock contention without a deadlock?
short: Blocking can occur even without a cycle when one transaction holds a resource for a long time.
answer: Identify the blocking session, SQL statement, transaction age and lock resource. Reduce transaction scope, add indexes, commit sooner or redesign access patterns.
followups: How do you find the blocker?
Can a slow query cause blocking?
interview: A lock wait is not automatically a deadlock. I find the blocker, inspect why its transaction is long, and fix the root cause rather than merely increasing timeouts.
scenario: Blocking can occur even without a cycle when one transaction holds a resource for a long time.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is OAuth2 PKCE and why is it important?
short: PKCE binds an authorization code exchange to a client-generated verifier.
answer: The client creates a verifier and sends its challenge to the authorization server. Later it must present the verifier to redeem the code, reducing the impact of an intercepted authorization code.
interview: PKCE protects the authorization-code flow by proving that the party redeeming the code started the flow. It is especially important for public clients.

title: What is OpenID Connect?
short: OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top of OAuth2.
answer: It defines an ID token and user identity claims so a client can authenticate a user, while OAuth2 itself primarily defines delegated authorization.
interview: OAuth2 answers what access a client gets; OpenID Connect adds standardized user authentication and identity claims.

title: How do you validate JWT claims beyond the signature?
short: Signature validation proves integrity, but a service must also validate claims relevant to its trust model.
answer: Check issuer, audience, expiry, not-before and required scopes/roles as appropriate. Algorithm and key selection must be constrained rather than blindly trusting token headers.
followups: Can a valid token still be unauthorized?
interview: I validate signature plus issuer, audience and time-based claims, then enforce scopes or roles for the requested operation.

title: What is token audience and why does it matter?
short: The audience identifies the intended recipient of a token.
answer: A service should reject a token minted for a different service even if its signature is valid. This limits token replay across APIs.
interview: A valid JWT is not automatically valid for every service. I check aud so a token intended for one API cannot be reused against another.

title: How should secrets be rotated without downtime?
short: Secret rotation should allow old and new credentials to overlap briefly while clients switch.
answer: Read new secrets from a managed store, reload them safely, and retire old credentials only after consumers have migrated. For signing keys, key IDs and overlapping public keys help.
followups: How do you rotate DB passwords?
How do you rotate JWT keys?
interview: I use versioned secrets and an overlap window. Rotation must be automated and observable so a credential change does not become an outage.

title: What is least privilege in backend authorization?
short: Least privilege grants only the permissions required for a task.
answer: Apply it to users, service identities, database roles and cloud IAM. Review permissions periodically and separate read, write and administrative actions.
followups: How do you review service permissions?
interview: I start with the minimum permissions required and grant broader access only when there is a documented need.

title: How do you prevent sensitive data from leaking into logs?
short: Sensitive fields should be excluded, masked or tokenized before logging.
answer: Define structured logging policies, redact authorization headers, passwords, tokens and personal data, and review exception logging paths because stack traces and request dumps can expose data.
followups: How do you redact nested objects?
What about debug logging in production?
interview: I use structured logs with explicit redaction and never log credentials or full sensitive payloads. Logging policy should be tested, not assumed.

title: What is SSRF DNS rebinding?
short: DNS rebinding can make a hostname resolve to a benign address during validation and a private address during the actual request.
answer: Mitigation requires validating the resolved address at connection time or using a trusted egress proxy/allowlist rather than trusting one DNS lookup.
interview: A URL allowlist based only on the initial DNS result can be bypassed. The network control must validate the actual destination or route requests through a controlled proxy.

title: What is replay attack protection for APIs?
short: Replay protection prevents an attacker from reusing a previously valid request or credential.
answer: Use short-lived tokens, nonce or timestamp validation for signed requests, idempotency keys for commands, TLS and server-side replay tracking where required.
interview: For sensitive commands I combine TLS with short-lived credentials and idempotency or nonce mechanisms so captured requests cannot simply be repeated.
scenario: Replay protection prevents an attacker from reusing a previously valid request or credential.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: How do you secure internal admin APIs?
short: Internal location alone should not be treated as sufficient authorization.
answer: Require strong identity, explicit authorization, network restrictions, audit logging and possibly step-up authentication for sensitive actions. Keep admin endpoints separate where practical.
followups: How do you audit admin actions?
interview: I protect admin APIs with strong authentication and fine-grained authorization even inside the network, then add network controls and audit trails as defense in depth.
scenario: Internal location alone should not be treated as sufficient authorization.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.

interview: I create a canonical representation for each word. Words with the same sorted characters belong to the same HashMap bucket. This gives average O(n * k log k) time when sorting each word.
problem: Given an array of strings, group all anagrams together.
example:
Input: [eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat]
Output: [[eat, tea, ate], [tan, nat], [bat]]
approach: Sort the characters of each word to form a canonical key, then use a HashMap from that key to the words sharing it.
complexity:
Time: O(n * k log k), where n is the number of words and k is the maximum word length.
Space: O(n * k) for grouped output and keys.

title: What is the difference between AtomicReference and synchronized state?
short: AtomicReference updates one reference atomically without a traditional monitor.
answer: AtomicReference uses CAS-style updates for a single reference. It is useful for lock-free state transitions, but if several fields must change together a monitor or another coordinated design may be clearer.
mistakes: Do not assume atomic reference updates make a multi-step workflow atomic.
interview: I choose AtomicReference when one state reference can be updated atomically. If the invariant spans multiple mutable fields, I prefer a lock or immutable state object swapped as one reference.

title: How do you avoid blocking calls in a reactive Spring application?
short: Blocking work can occupy reactive event-loop threads and destroy throughput.
answer: Reactive applications rely on a small number of event-loop threads. Blocking JDBC, file I/O or long CPU work on those threads can stall unrelated requests. Blocking work should use an appropriate scheduler or, preferably, a non-blocking client.
followups: How do you detect blocking calls?
interview: In WebFlux I keep the event loop non-blocking. If a legacy blocking dependency cannot be replaced, I isolate it on a bounded scheduler and monitor its queue and latency rather than blocking event-loop threads.

title: How would you handle duplicate webhook delivery at the receiver?
short: Webhook receivers should assume the same event can arrive more than once.
answer: Use the provider's stable event ID as an idempotency key, persist processing state with a unique constraint, and return success for an already completed event. Keep the transaction that changes business state and records the event ID atomic where possible.
followups: What if processing crashes after the business update?
Should the receiver return 2xx for a duplicate?
interview: I treat webhook delivery as at-least-once. The receiver stores a unique event ID and makes the business update idempotent, so a retry returns the same outcome instead of applying the business change twice.
